paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.10:1 Rule 2.10 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.10. 1. Intervenors In UAlberta Pro-Life v. Governors of the University of Alberta, 2018 ABCA 350, 2018 CarswellAlta 2440, Justice Schutz gave this summary of the law governing the granting of intervenor status: [8] Rules 14.37(2)(e) and 14.58 of the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta Reg 124/2010 authorize a single judge to consider an application to intervene and to impose conditions. As an exercise of discretion, intervenor status should be granted sparingly: Telus Communications Inc v Telecommunications Workers Union, 2006 ABCA 297 (CanLII) at para 4, 401 AR 57 [Telus]; Pedersen v Alberta, 2008 ABCA 192 (CanLII) at para 4, 432 AR 219 [Pedersen]. [9] Generally, the Court must first consider the subject matter of the proceeding and then determine the proposed intervenor's interest in that subject matter: Papaschase Indian Band (Descendants of) v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320 (CanLII) at para 5, 380 AR 301 [Papaschase]. A proposed intervenor's interest in the subject matter is determined by assessing the following considerations: a. whether the proposed intervenor would be directly and “specially” affected by the outcome of the appeal or, b. whether the proposed intervenor has special expertise or a unique perspective relating to the subject matter of the appeal that will assist the Court in its deliberations. Papaschase at para 2; Telus at para 4; Edmonton (City) v Edmonton (Subdivision and Development Appeal Board), 2014 ABCA 340 (CanLII) at para 8, 584 AR 255 [Edmonton (City)]. [10] The following questions are also relevant to the consideration of whether an intervenor application ought to be granted: 1. Is the presence of the intervenor necessary for the court to properly decide the matter? 2. Might the intervenor's interest in the proceedings not be fully protected by the parties? 3. Will the intervention unduly delay the proceedings? 4. Will there possibly be prejudice to the parties if intervention is granted? 5. Will intervention widen the dispute between the parties? 6. Will the intervention transform the court into a political arena? Pedersen at para 3; Edmonton (City) at paras 8–14; Stewart Estate (Re), 2014 ABCA 222 (CanLII) at para 5, 577 AR 57; Styles v Canadian Association of Counsel for Employers, 2016 ABCA 218 (CanLII) at paras 13–15. [11] Further, if intervenor status is granted, an intervenor may not raise or argue issues not raised by the parties to the appeal unless otherwise ordered: Rule 14.58(3). Finally, a proposed intervenor should define the question on which they wish to intervene with particularity: R v Neve, 1996 ABCA 242 (CanLII) at para 16, 184 AR 359. In R. v. Hirsekorn, 2011 ABQB 156, 2011 CarswellAlta 393, [2011] 2 C.N.L.R. 269, Chief Justice Wittmann discussed applications for intervenor status. paragraphs.text: 13 In Papaschase Indian Band v. Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320, Chief Justice Fraser, speaking for the Court, said at para. 2: It may be fairly stated that, as a general principle, an intervention may be allowed where the proposed intervenor is specially affected by the decision facing the Court or the proposed intervenor has some special expertise or insight to bring to bear on the issues facing the court. She went on at para. 3 to cite Batchewana Indian Band v. Canada (Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs) (1996), 199 N.R. (F.C.A.) 1 where it was stated “… an Intervenor in an appellate court must take the case as she finds it and cannot, to the prejudice of the parties, argue new issues which require the introduction of fresh evidence.” 14 para. 5 of Papaschase is also instructive referring to a two-step approach to the determination of an Intervenor application where it is stated that the Court typically considers first the subject matter of the proceeding and second determines the proposed Intervenor's interest in the subject matter. 15 Another principle articulated at para. 6 of Papaschase is that where cases involve constitutional issues or which have a “constitutional dimension”, courts are generally more lenient in granting Intervenor status. In Peavine Metis Settlement v. Alberta (Minister of Energy), 2011 ABQB 472, 2011 CarswellAlta 1258, 23 C.P.C. (7th) 174, at paragraphs 9-10, Justice Browne referred with approval to R. v. Hirsekorn. In University of Alberta v. Alberta (Information & Privacy Commissioner), 2011 ABQB 389, 2011 CarswellAlta 1043, 55 Alta. L.R. (5th) 131; additional reasons at 2011 CarswellAlta 1320, 2011 ABQB 486, 58 Alta. L.R. (5th) 415, Justice Lee, at paragraph 14, referred with approval to Hirsekorn, and went on to say, at paragraph 16: 16 Lefsrud J in Smyth v. Edmonton (City) Police Service, 2005 ABQB 652 discussed the two part test to be applied in an intervenor application, and noted (at paras. 15-16): To determine whether a party should be permitted to intervene, the Court must apply a two step process. (Ahyasou v. Lund, [1998] A.J. No. 1154 (Q.B.) referred to with approval by the Court of Appeal in the Alberta (Minister of Justice) v. Métis Settlements Appeal Tribunal[2005] A.J. No. 362, 2005 ABCA 143). The first step is to characterize the subject matter of the proceedings, and the second step is to determine what interest, if any, the proposed intervenor has in it. The Alberta Court of Appeal in the Metis Settlements endorsed the following three grounds for determining whether the proposed intervenor has sufficient interest in the subject matter. Those grounds are whether the Applicant: 1. will be specially affected by the decision facing the Court; 2. has some special expertise or insight to bring to bear on the issues facing the Court, or 3. has interests that may not be fully protected by the parties. In Alberta Sports & Recreation Assn. for the Blind v. Edmonton (City) (1993), 14 Alta. L.R. (3d) 301 (Q.B.), at 302-304, Ritter J. said: It is conceded by all parties that the Court has jurisdiction to grant intervenor status as this status was historically exercised by the English Chancery Court. In addition ss. 4 and 5 of the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 1980, c. J-1, confirm inherent jurisdiction to allow a non-party to intervene in matters before the Court… It is clear that intervenor status has traditionally been granted where a non-party applicant has an interest in the actual dispute between the parties … It is also clear that where there is a challenge to legislation pursuant to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the courts are prepared to give a less stringent interpretation of the normal requirements for intervenor status. In C.L.C. v. Bhindi (1985), 17 D.L.R. (4th) 193 (B.C. C.A.), Anderson J.A. discusses the role of intervenors and notes that [p. 203]: (2) The evidence adduced in respect of s. 1 of the Charter should be introduced at the trial level. In fact, as a matter of practice, all documentary evidence should be made available to the opposite ‘parties’ or ‘intervenors’ prior to trial. If any of the ‘parties’ or ‘intervenors’ are desirous of calling expert witnesses, summaries of the evidence sought to be introduced by expert witnesses should also be made available to the opposite ‘parties’ or ‘intervenors’ prior to the relevancy or admissibility of documentary or viva voce evidence would be dealt with by the trial judge. The courts have consistently stated that the application of s. 1 of the Charter requires evidence. If that evidence is either within the abilities of a proposed intervenor or its adduction can be assisted by a proposed intervenor, then it is not unreasonable to presume that the difficulties with application of s. 1 of the Charter can more readily be avoided. Further Anderson J.A. at p. 204 of C.L.C. v. Bhindi, supra, states: I would add on this point, that it is important in dealing with Charter issues raised for the first time, that the courts have the assistance of argument from all segments of the community. The courts should not resist but should welcome such assistance. Further at p. 205 of C.L.C. v. Bhindi, supra, Anderson J.A. states: (6) While no doubt the intervention of the appellant will add to the length and complexity of the trial, the additional expense is on balance, justified. Issues relating to s. 1 of the Charter cannot and should not be addressed in a vacuum. The defendant suggests that the applicants must show some unique position which is different from that of the defendant. This matter was also raised in C.L.C. v. Bhindi, supra, and at pp. 203-204, Anderson J.A. states: (4) No authority has been offered in support of the argument that before intervenor status will be granted, the applicant must show that its interests differ from the interests of the Union. On the contrary, in the Supreme Court of Canada, ‘intervenor’ status will be granted in constitutional cases where the proposed ‘intervenor’ can show that its interests will be affected by the outcome of the litigation; see, for example, Law Society of Upper Canada v. Skapinker (1984), 9 D.L.R. (4th) 161 … where the Federation of Law Societies of Canada was given leave to intervene. … The plaintiff also argued that the proposed intervenors have not consulted with the defendants to determine whether the defendants would likely be raising the same defences in any event and whether the defendants would be prepared to advance the proposed intervenor's position to the Court. Again, this matter was dealt with by Anderson J.A. in C.L.C. v. Bhindi, supra, and at p. 206 he states: (7) While it is possible that the Union could employ counsel employed by the appellant and conduct its defence in accordance with the wishes of the appellant, it is not for the courts to interfere in such matters. In Suncor Energy Inc. v. Unifor, Local 707 A, 2014 ABQB 555, 2014 CarswellAlta 1655, Chief Justice Wittmann summarized the matters to be considered on an application for intervenor status. At paragraphs 7-8, his Lordship said: [7] Although the Alberta Rules of Court (“ARC”) in ARC 2.10 provide that a Court may grant status to a person to intervene subject to any terms and conditions and with the rights and privileges specified by the Court, no test is set forth to guide the Court in intervention applications. The common law governs. [8] None of the parties disputes the test to guide judicial discretion. As set forth in the Applicants' brief, the considerations are as follows: 1. Will the proposed interveners be specially or directly affected by the decision of the Court: Papaschase Indian Band v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320 (CanLII), [2005] AJ No 1273 at paragraph 2; Knox v. Conservative Party of Canada, 2007 ABCA 141 (CanLII) at paragraph 5; Alberta (Minister of Justice) v Metis Settlements Appeals Tribunal, 2005 ABCA 143 (CanLII) at paragraph 4; R v Finta, 1993 CanLII 132 (SCC), [1993] 1 SCR 1138 at 1143; Carbon Development Partnership v Alberta (Energy and Utilities Board), 2007 ABCA 231 (CanLII), [2007] AJ No 727 at paragraph 10. 2. Will the proposed interveners bring special expertise or insight to bear on the issues facing the Court: Papaschase at paragraph 2; Goudreau v Falher Consolidated School District No 69, 1993 ABCA 72 at paragraph 17. This question is akin to whether an intervener would provide “fresh information or fresh perspective”. Reference Re Workers' Compensation Act, 1983 (Nfld), 1989 CanLII 23 (SCC), [1989] 2 SCR 335 at 340; Stewart Estate (Re), 2014 ABCA 222 (CanLII) at paragraph 7. 3. Are the proposed interveners' interests at risk of not being fully protected or fully argued by one of the parties: United Taxi Drivers' Fellowship of Southern Alberta v Calgary (City), 202 ABCA 243 at paragraph 2; Gift Lake Metis Settlement v. Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2008 ABCA 391 (CanLII) at paragraph 6; Metis Settlements Appeal Tribunal at paragraph 4. 4. Will the interveners presence “provide the Court with fresh information or a fresh perspective on a constitutional or public issue”Reference Re Workers' Compensation Act at 340; Papaschase at paragraph 9. Another factor is whether granting a right to intervene would unduly prejudice a party. In Athabasca Tribal Council v. Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) (1998), 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 232 (Q.B.), Mr. Justice Medhurst gave the following summary of the law relating to intervenors (at p. 236): Whether or not a party can intervene in an action is a matter that is to be decided at the discretion of the judge hearing the application. While many Canadian jurisdictions have rules which specify conditions in which intervenor status will be granted, Alberta has no such rules and reference must be had to the common law. The test developed in the common law is essentially that a party should only be granted intervenor status if the party will be directly affected by the ultimate decision of the case and/or where the presence of the party is necessary for the Court to properly decide the matter. . . . . . In making a determination on this issue, a two step approach is appropriate: “The first step is to characterize the subject-matter or the nature of the proceeding. The second step is to determine what interest the proposed intervenor has in it.” (P. Muldoon Law of Intervention Status and Practice (Ontario: Canada Law Books Inc. 1989) at 40.) In R. v. Trang, 2002 ABQB 185, 2002 CarswellAlta 247, 4 Alta. L.R. (4th) 161, Marceau J., referred with approval to Athabasca Tribal Council v. Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) (1998), 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 232 (Q.B.), and then said (at pp. 167-168): A line of cases at the Federal Court has stated that a proposed intervenor must have more than a jurisprudential interest in order to intervene in a particular case. … In R. v. Boulton, [1976] 1 F.C. 252 (Fed. C.A.), Jackett C.J. explained this concept at 253: In our view, no matter how widely one interprets the Court's power to permit persons to be heard, it does not extend to permit a person to be heard merely because he has an interest in another controversy where the same question of law will or may arise as that which will or may arise in the controversy that is before the Court. There are cases that indicate that an organization may have a sufficiently direct interest to be granted intervenor status if it represents those who themselves have a substantial interest in the matter. … However, there ought to be a distinction made between the case of a parent organization whose members are affected by a decision and that of an organization of lawyers whose members are not affected by a decision but whose members represent those who are. … … Therefore, the ultimate test is that stated in [Athabasca Tribal Council, supra]: the proposed intervenor will either have a direct interest (not a merely jurisprudential one) or its presence will be necessary for a decision (because its expertise will be of assistance). In P. (N.) v. LDS Adoption Services, 2006 ABQB 78, 2006 CarswellAlta 126, 392 A.R. 282, 57 Alta. L.R. (4th) 59, Langston J. said, at pp. 77-78: In Alberta, in contrast to some other jurisdictions, there are no specific rules with respect to intervenor status and resort must be had to the common law. Oddly enough, the test that has been applied appears to be substantially similar to the test for determining party status. In W.A. Stevenson & J.E. Côté, Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol. 1 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2003) it is said at p. 10-11 that “The test [for intervention in private disputes] is whether the proposed intervener would be directly affected by the decision, and whether its presence is necessary for the court properly to decide the matter.” This was also the view taken by Gallant J. of this Court in Veterinary Medical Assn. (Alberta) v. Pequin, 2002 ABQB 115 (Alta. Q.B.). Two interesting cases out of Manitoba indicate that the second criterion requires the proposed intervenor to demonstrate that it will bring before the court something that will not be brought forward by the parties. In Klachefsky v. Brown (1987), [1988] 1 W.W.R. 755 (Man. C.A.), the Women's Legal Education and Action Fund sought intervenor status to raise the issue of sexual equality in a custody matter. The trial judge refused and the Manitoba Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, making the following comments at p. 758: Counsel for the wife is entirely capable of raising and ventilating any issue relative to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms should counsel consider that such an argument would advance the cause of her client. … I can well understand an intervention where counsel for one of the parties is unwilling or unable to raise an issue of substance which could affect the development of the law in future cases. Those are not the circumstances here. Counsel for the wife labours under no restraints in raising those arguments which might find favour with the court, including any argument based upon Charter principles. The intervention of a third party into what is essentially a private dispute is not to be lightly entertained. An intervention adds unnecessarily to the cost of proceedings and might well also add to the length of litigation. It constitutes an inconvenience to the parties which ought not to be imposed upon them except under compelling circumstances, which do not exist in this case. In Mr. Pawn Ltd. v. Winnipeg (City) (1998), [1999] 2 W.W.R. 521 (Man. Q.B.), a community interest organization sought to intervene in an application challenging the city's authority to pass certain by-laws relating to pawn shops. Steel J. noted at p. 524 that it was not clear that the community group would make arguments different from those made by the city, but that the group took the position that its concerns were unique: Counsel did not identify a specific argument or issue that would be advanced by the intervenor over and above the proposed argument by the City of Winnipeg. The intervenor indicated that at the present time it was not familiar with all the arguments that might be presented on behalf of the City, nor had it decided upon the extent of its own arguments. Rather, the intervenor contended that it would be placing emphasis on different points of law or different cases than might be put forward by the City of Winnipeg. This argument may be summarized by referring to Reverend Lehotsky's affidavit where he states: We believe that the neighbourhood affected by this Application has unique and special concerns that may not necessarily be expressed by the City of Winnipeg, as the latter can be expected to take a position and frame its arguments on behalf of the whole city and all its constituents. For example, we believe that the pawn-shop licensing by-law can and should be interpreted in a manner that affords greater scope for public participation in decision-making, enables the City of Winnipeg to consider the density of pawnshops in a particular area in determining whether granting such license (sic) is injurious to the public interest, and takes greater account of Plan Winnipeg, the City's main planning document. Though he acknowledged that the extent to which a proposed intervenor's interests must diverge from those of the parties will depend upon the circumstances of the case, Steel J. found at p. 529 that there must be some difference in the arguments sought to be made: Depending on the circumstances, it may not be necessary for the proposed intervenor to put forward a substantially different issue. In Charter cases, for example, different nuances in argument may be important to be heard, not because they affect the outcome of the case but because they may affect the reasons for decisions and therefore the precedential authority of the case. Where policy issues are being decided within a Charter of Rights framework, presentations that provide different perspectives and assist in identifying consequences and ramifications can be especially helpful to the courts. . . . . . Yet, no purpose is served by having intervenors duplicate the arguments of the parties. At a minimum, the applicants must be able to show how their submissions will be useful and different from those of the other parties in some way. 2. Public Interest Standing In Scenic Acres Community Assn. v. Calgary (City), 2015 ABQB 586, a community association sought a declaration that the Calgary Board of Education had violated s. 672 of the Municipal Government Act (Alberta) in transferring a particular parcel of land to different school region. The issue determined by Justice D. B. Nixon was whether the community association had standing to bring the action. His Lordship said: 44 The threshold question in this case is whether the Community Association has standing to advance this matter in this Court. The Defendants assert that the Community Association lacks the necessary standing to maintain this application because it is not specially and particularly affected by the decision of City Council to approve the transfer of the Lands jointly to the City and FrancoSud. The Defendants cite Finlay v Canada, [1986] 2 SCR 607 in support of this proposition. 45 It is clear that the Community Association has no specific standing. Accordingly, the next question is whether the Community Association satisfies the “public interest standing” threshold. 46 The law in Canada in respect of “public interest standing” has changed over the decades. In recent years, the Courts have taken a more liberal approach to the concept. While the Finlay decision relied upon by the Defendants is instructive, Canada (AG) v Downtown Eastside Sex Workers, 2012 SCC 45, [2012] 2 S.C.R. 524 is more relevant because it updates the law in this area. 47 In Downtown Eastside, Justice Cromwell commented that Canadian courts have relaxed limitations on public interest standing. In particular, he commented that the Courts have taken a flexible, discretionary approach to public interest standing and are to be guided by the purposes which underlie the traditional limitations: Downtown Eastside, at para 1. 48 In analyzing the appropriate boundaries of “public interest standing”, Justice Cromwell commented at paras 35-36: The decision to grant or refuse standing involves the careful exercise of judicial discretion through the weighing of the three factors (serious justiciable issue, the nature of the plaintiff's interest, and other reasonable and effective means [of bringing the issue before the court]) … … the factors should be seen as interrelated considerations to be weighed cumulatively, not individually, and in light of their purposes. 49 The most significant shift that Downtown Eastside brought to the “public interest standing” framework was in respect of the third factor. In his consideration of this factor, Justice Cromwell indicated that the question should be whether the proposed suit is a reasonable and effective means to bring the challenge to court. He further indicated that this “… approach to the third factor better reflects the flexible, discretionary and purposive approach to public interest standing that underpins all of the Court's decisions in this area”: Downtown Eastside, at para 44. 50 The effect of that judicial comment was to make it clear that the strict requirement outlined by the majority in Minister of Justice v Borowski, [1981] 2 SCR 575 no longer applied. In Borowski, the majority held at page 598 that the person seeking standing had “… to show … that there [was]…no other reasonable effective manner in which the issue may be brought before the Court” (emphasis added). 1. —Three Factors 51 Given this updated judicial framework, the facts must be considered in the context of these three enumerated factors to determine whether the Community Association should be granted “public interest standing”. a. —The First Factor—Serious Justiciable Issue 52 In Downtown Eastside at para 42, the Supreme Court confirmed its holding in Finlay that, to constitute a serious issue, a claim must be “far from frivolous”. However, the courts need not examine the merits of the case in “other than a preliminary manner”. … b. —The Second Factor—The Nature of the Plaintiff's Interest 57 The second factor is “whether the party bringing the action has a real stake or a genuine interest in its outcome” (emphasis added): Downtown Eastside, at para 2. The purpose underlying this factor “… reflects the concern for conserving scarce judicial resources …”: Downtown Eastside, at para 43, referencing Finlay at page 633. … c. —The Third Factor—Reasonable and Effective Means 64 Notwithstanding the above determination concerning the second factor, the Supreme Court of Canada's direction in Downtown Eastside is that all factors be considered cumulatively. Accordingly, a review of the third factor is required. 65 The Community Association seeks relief under the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 2000, c.J-2 (the “Judicature Act”) and the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010 (the “Rules of Court”). It has chosen this procedure rather than seeking a judicial review or filing an objection under the MGA, which has a specific appeal provision. 66 This Court is not satisfied that the procedure chosen by the Community Association is the only “reasonable and effective means of bringing the issue[s] before the Court”. Other appeal mechanisms were available, but were not pursued. That being the case, the third factor has not been satisfied. 3. Party status? In Auer v. Auer, 2018 ABQB 510, 2018 CarswellAlta 1309, 73 Alta. L.R. (6th) 153, 11 R.F.L. (8th) 338, [2018] 9 W.W.R. 744, the Attorney General of Canada applied for intervenor status in a matter in which one of the parties sought a declaration that the Federal Child Support Guidelines were ultra vires the Divorce Act (Canada). Justice Gates granted that application, and then had to decide the extent to which the Attorney General would be allowed to participate in the action. His Lordship granted what he termed “party-like status”. Gates, J. said: 126 Rule 2.10 is silent on the scope of intervention that is appropriate when a court grants intervenor status pursuant to this rule. Rule 2.10 does not specify whether this Court has the power to grant the Attorney General the status of a full party. 127 The Attorney General relies on the Ontario decision in North American Financial Group Inc v Ontario (Securities Commission), 2017 ONSC 2965, as support for the argument that she is entitled to party status. However, in Stratum Projects Alberta Inc v Aman Building Corp, 2017 ABQB 351 at paras 21–28, Master Schlosser notes that the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, RRO 1990, Reg 194, explicitly allow for intervention as an added party, whereas the Alberta Rules of Court do not contain similarly explicit language. As such, Master Schlosser questions whether Rule 2.10 contemplates granting party status to an intervenor. 128 Generally, Alberta case law cautions that the scope of any intervention should be limited to only what is required for a court to make a proper determination on the issues before it: R v Hirsekorn, 2011 ABQB 156 at para 21. An intervenor should generally not be allowed to introduce new issues or enlarge the issues already before the court. In the current circumstances, however, where this Court is faced with an otherwise unopposed challenge to the vires of the Guidelines, the Attorney General is, in my view, entitled to participate fully in this process. 129 Accordingly, the Attorney General of Canada is granted intervenor status with rights and duties comparable to that of a party, which includes: (a) The right to cross-examine on the previously specified affidavits for no more than one day; (b) The right to make oral and/or written submissions on any aspect of the vires application, including evidentiary and jurisdictional issues; (c) The right to put public documents before the Court to establish legislative and social facts concerning the development and implementation of the Guidelines; and (d) The right to appeal an adverse decision. 130 The Attorney General's right to appeal stems from the Alberta Rules of Court, which allows appeals from a party to an action heard before the Court of Queen's Bench: Peavine Metis Settlement v Whitehead, 2015 ABCA 366 at paras 50–52. 131 It is also applicable regardless of whether Rule 2.10 contemplates an intervenor being given party status. Even if Rule 2.10 does not contemplate party status, I would still grant the Attorney General party-like status, including the right to appeal, due to the extraordinary nature of Dr. Auer's otherwise unopposed vires challenge to the Guidelines. 4. Costs for Intervenors See the annotation “Costs for Intervenors” under Rule 10.31. Generally see: Imperial Oil Ltd. v. Alberta (Minister of Environment), 2005 ABCA 375, 2005 CarswellAlta 1595 at paragraph 25.

L.R.
(5th) 131; additional reasons at 2011 CarswellAlta 1320, 2011 ABQB 486, 58 Alta.
L.R.
(5th) 415, Justice Lee, at paragraph 14, referred with approval to Hirsekorn, and went on to say, at paragraph 16: 16 Lefsrud J in Smyth v.
Edmonton (City) Police Service, 2005 ABQB 652 discussed the two part test to be applied in an intervenor application, and noted (at paras.
15-16): To determine whether a party should be permitted to intervene, the Court must apply a two step process.
(Ahyasou v.
Lund, [1998] A.J.
No.
1154 (Q.B.) referred to with approval by the Court of Appeal in the Alberta (Minister of Justice) v.
Métis Settlements Appeal Tribunal[2005] A.J.
No.
The first step is to characterize the subject matter of the proceedings, and the second step is to determine what interest, if any, the proposed intervenor has in it.
The Alberta Court of Appeal in the Metis Settlements endorsed the following three grounds for determining whether the proposed intervenor has sufficient interest in the subject matter.

Those grounds are whether the Applicant: 1. will be specially affected by the decision facing the Court; 2. has some special expertise or insight to bring to bear on the issues facing the Court, or 3. has interests that may not be fully protected by the parties.
In Alberta Sports & Recreation Assn. for the Blind v.
Edmonton (City) (1993), 14 Alta.
L.R.

(3d) 301 (Q.B.), at 302-304, Ritter J. said: It is conceded by all parties that the Court has jurisdiction to grant intervenor status as this status was historically exercised by the English Chancery Court.
In addition ss.
4 and 5 of the Judicature Act, R.S.A.

J-1, confirm inherent jurisdiction to allow a non-party to intervene in matters before the Court… It is clear that intervenor status has traditionally been granted where a non-party applicant has an interest in the actual dispute between the parties … It is also clear that where there is a challenge to legislation pursuant to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, the courts are prepared to give a less stringent interpretation of the normal requirements for intervenor status.
In C.L.C. v.
Bhindi (1985), 17 D.L.R.
C.A.), Anderson J.A. discusses the role of intervenors and notes that [p.
203]: (2) The evidence adduced in respect of s.
1 of the Charter should be introduced at the trial level.
In fact, as a matter of practice, all documentary evidence should be made available to the opposite ‘parties’ or ‘intervenors’ prior to trial.

If any of the ‘parties’ or ‘intervenors’ are desirous of calling expert witnesses, summaries of the evidence sought to be introduced by expert witnesses should also be made available to the opposite ‘parties’ or ‘intervenors’ prior to the relevancy or admissibility of documentary or viva voce evidence would be dealt with by the trial judge.
The courts have consistently stated that the application of s.
1 of the Charter requires evidence.

If that evidence is either within the abilities of a proposed intervenor or its adduction can be assisted by a proposed intervenor, then it is not unreasonable to presume that the difficulties with application of s.
1 of the Charter can more readily be avoided.
Further Anderson J.A. at p.
204 of C.L.C. v.

Bhindi, supra, states: I would add on this point, that it is important in dealing with Charter issues raised for the first time, that the courts have the assistance of argument from all segments of the community.
The courts should not resist but should welcome such assistance.
Further at p.
205 of C.L.C. v.
Bhindi, supra, Anderson J.A. states: (6) While no doubt the intervention of the appellant will add to the length and complexity of the trial, the additional expense is on balance, justified.
Issues relating to s.
1 of the Charter cannot and should not be addressed in a vacuum.
The defendant suggests that the applicants must show some unique position which is different from that of the defendant.
This matter was also raised in C.L.C. v.
Bhindi, supra, and at pp.

203-204, Anderson J.A. states: (4) No authority has been offered in support of the argument that before intervenor status will be granted, the applicant must show that its interests differ from the interests of the Union.

On the contrary, in the Supreme Court of Canada, ‘intervenor’ status will be granted in constitutional cases where the proposed ‘intervenor’ can show that its interests will be affected by the outcome of the litigation; see, for example, Law Society of Upper Canada v.
Skapinker (1984), 9 D.L.R.

(4th) 161 … where the Federation of Law Societies of Canada was given leave to intervene. … The plaintiff also argued that the proposed intervenors have not consulted with the defendants to determine whether the defendants would likely be raising the same defences in any event and whether the defendants would be prepared to advance the proposed intervenor's position to the Court.
Again, this matter was dealt with by Anderson J.A. in C.L.C. v.
Bhindi, supra, and at p.

206 he states: (7) While it is possible that the Union could employ counsel employed by the appellant and conduct its defence in accordance with the wishes of the appellant, it is not for the courts to interfere in such matters.
In Suncor Energy Inc. v.
Unifor, Local 707 A, 2014 ABQB 555, 2014 CarswellAlta 1655, Chief Justice Wittmann summarized the matters to be considered on an application for intervenor status.

At paragraphs 7-8, his Lordship said: [7] Although the Alberta Rules of Court (“ARC”) in ARC 2.10 provide that a Court may grant status to a person to intervene subject to any terms and conditions and with the rights and privileges specified by the Court, no test is set forth to guide the Court in intervention applications.
The common law governs.
[8] None of the parties disputes the test to guide judicial discretion.
As set forth in the Applicants' brief, the considerations are as follows: 1.

Will the proposed interveners be specially or directly affected by the decision of the Court: Papaschase Indian Band v Canada (Attorney General), 2005 ABCA 320 (CanLII), [2005] AJ No 1273 at paragraph 2; Knox v.
Conservative Party of Canada, 2007 ABCA 141 (CanLII) at paragraph 5
Alberta (Minister of Justice) v Metis Settlements Appeals Tribunal, 2005 ABCA 143 (CanLII) at paragraph 4
R v Finta, 1993 CanLII 132 (SCC), [1993] 1 SCR 1138 at 1143
Carbon Development Partnership v Alberta (Energy and Utilities Board), 2007 ABCA 231 (CanLII), [2007] AJ No 727 at paragraph 10.

Will the proposed interveners bring special expertise or insight to bear on the issues facing the Court: Papaschase at paragraph 2; Goudreau v Falher Consolidated School District No 69, 1993 ABCA 72 at paragraph 17.
This question is akin to whether an intervener would provide “fresh information or fresh perspective”.
Reference Re Workers' Compensation Act, 1983 (Nfld), 1989 CanLII 23 (SCC), [1989] 2 SCR 335 at 340; Stewart Estate (Re), 2014 ABCA 222 (CanLII) at paragraph 7.

Are the proposed interveners' interests at risk of not being fully protected or fully argued by one of the parties: United Taxi Drivers' Fellowship of Southern Alberta v Calgary (City), 202 ABCA 243 at paragraph 2
Gift Lake Metis Settlement v.
Canadian Natural Resources Limited, 2008 ABCA 391 (CanLII) at paragraph 6; Metis Settlements Appeal Tribunal at paragraph 4.

Will the interveners presence “provide the Court with fresh information or a fresh perspective on a constitutional or public issue”Reference Re Workers' Compensation Act at 340; Papaschase at paragraph 9.
Another factor is whether granting a right to intervene would unduly prejudice a party.
In Athabasca Tribal Council v.
Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) (1998), 67 Alta.
L.R.
Justice Medhurst gave the following summary of the law relating to intervenors (at p.
236): Whether or not a party can intervene in an action is a matter that is to be decided at the discretion of the judge hearing the application.
While many Canadian jurisdictions have rules which specify conditions in which intervenor status will be granted, Alberta has no such rules and reference must be had to the common law.

The test developed in the common law is essentially that a party should only be granted intervenor status if the party will be directly affected by the ultimate decision of the case and/or where the presence of the party is necessary for the Court to properly decide the matter. . . . . .
In making a determination on this issue, a two step approach is appropriate: “The first step is to characterize the subject-matter or the nature of the proceeding.
The second step is to determine what interest the proposed intervenor has in it.” (P.
Muldoon Law of Intervention Status and Practice (Ontario: Canada Law Books Inc.
Trang, 2002 ABQB 185, 2002 CarswellAlta 247, 4 Alta.
L.R.
(4th) 161, Marceau J., referred with approval to Athabasca Tribal Council v.
Alberta (Minister of Environmental Protection) (1998), 67 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 232 (Q.B.), and then said (at pp.
167-168): A line of cases at the Federal Court has stated that a proposed intervenor must have more than a jurisprudential interest in order to intervene in a particular case. … In R. v.
Boulton, [1976] 1 F.C.

C.A.), Jackett C.J. explained this concept at 253: In our view, no matter how widely one interprets the Court's power to permit persons to be heard, it does not extend to permit a person to be heard merely because he has an interest in another controversy where the same question of law will or may arise as that which will or may arise in the controversy that is before the Court.

There are cases that indicate that an organization may have a sufficiently direct interest to be granted intervenor status if it represents those who themselves have a substantial interest in the matter. … However, there ought to be a distinction made between the case of a parent organization whose members are affected by a decision and that of an organization of lawyers whose members are not affected by a decision but whose members represent those who are. … … Therefore, the ultimate test is that stated in [Athabasca Tribal Council, supra]: the proposed intervenor will either have a direct interest (not a merely jurisprudential one) or its presence will be necessary for a decision (because its expertise will be of assistance).
In P.
LDS Adoption Services, 2006 ABQB 78, 2006 CarswellAlta 126, 392 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 59, Langston J. said, at pp.
77-78: In Alberta, in contrast to some other jurisdictions, there are no specific rules with respect to intervenor status and resort must be had to the common law.
Oddly enough, the test that has been applied appears to be substantially similar to the test for determining party status.
In W.A.
Stevenson & J.E.
Côté, Civil Procedure Encyclopedia, vol.
1 (Edmonton: Juriliber, 2003) it is said at p.

10-11 that “The test [for intervention in private disputes] is whether the proposed intervener would be directly affected by the decision, and whether its presence is necessary for the court properly to decide the matter.” This was also the view taken by Gallant J. of this Court in Veterinary Medical Assn.
(Alberta) v.
Pequin, 2002 ABQB 115 (Alta.

Two interesting cases out of Manitoba indicate that the second criterion requires the proposed intervenor to demonstrate that it will bring before the court something that will not be brought forward by the parties.
In Klachefsky v.
C.A.), the Women's Legal Education and Action Fund sought intervenor status to raise the issue of sexual equality in a custody matter.
The trial judge refused and the Manitoba Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, making the following comments at p.

758: Counsel for the wife is entirely capable of raising and ventilating any issue relative to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms should counsel consider that such an argument would advance the cause of her client. … I can well understand an intervention where counsel for one of the parties is unwilling or unable to raise an issue of substance which could affect the development of the law in future cases.
Those are not the circumstances here.
Counsel for the wife labours under no restraints in raising those arguments which might find favour with the court, including any argument based upon Charter principles.
The intervention of a third party into what is essentially a private dispute is not to be lightly entertained.
An intervention adds unnecessarily to the cost of proceedings and might well also add to the length of litigation.
It constitutes an inconvenience to the parties which ought not to be imposed upon them except under compelling circumstances, which do not exist in this case.
In Mr.
Pawn Ltd. v.
Winnipeg (City) (1998), [1999] 2 W.W.R.
Q.B.), a community interest organization sought to intervene in an application challenging the city's authority to pass certain by-laws relating to pawn shops.
Steel J. noted at p.

524 that it was not clear that the community group would make arguments different from those made by the city, but that the group took the position that its concerns were unique: Counsel did not identify a specific argument or issue that would be advanced by the intervenor over and above the proposed argument by the City of Winnipeg.
The intervenor indicated that at the present time it was not familiar with all the arguments that might be presented on behalf of the City, nor had it decided upon the extent of its own arguments.
Rather, the intervenor contended that it would be placing emphasis on different points of law or different cases than might be put forward by the City of Winnipeg.

This argument may be summarized by referring to Reverend Lehotsky's affidavit where he states: We believe that the neighbourhood affected by this Application has unique and special concerns that may not necessarily be expressed by the City of Winnipeg, as the latter can be expected to take a position and frame its arguments on behalf of the whole city and all its constituents.

For example, we believe that the pawn-shop licensing by-law can and should be interpreted in a manner that affords greater scope for public participation in decision-making, enables the City of Winnipeg to consider the density of pawnshops in a particular area in determining whether granting such license
(sic) is injurious to the public interest, and takes greater account of Plan Winnipeg, the City's main planning document.
Though he acknowledged that the extent to which a proposed intervenor's interests must diverge from those of the parties will depend upon the circumstances of the case, Steel J. found at p.

529 that there must be some difference in the arguments sought to be made: Depending on the circumstances, it may not be necessary for the proposed intervenor to put forward a substantially different issue.

In Charter cases, for example, different nuances in argument may be important to be heard, not because they affect the outcome of the case but because they may affect the reasons for decisions and therefore the precedential authority of the case.

Where policy issues are being decided within a Charter of Rights framework, presentations that provide different perspectives and assist in identifying consequences and ramifications can be especially helpful to the courts. . . . . .
Yet, no purpose is served by having intervenors duplicate the arguments of the parties.
At a minimum, the applicants must be able to show how their submissions will be useful and different from those of the other parties in some way.
Public Interest Standing In Scenic Acres Community Assn. v.
Calgary (City), 2015 ABQB 586, a community association sought a declaration that the Calgary Board of Education had violated s.
672 of the Municipal Government Act (Alberta) in transferring a particular parcel of land to different school region.
The issue determined by Justice D.
B.
Nixon was whether the community association had standing to bring the action.
His Lordship said: 44 The threshold question in this case is whether the Community Association has standing to advance this matter in this Court.

The Defendants assert that the Community Association lacks the necessary standing to maintain this application because it is not specially and particularly affected by the decision of City Council to approve the transfer of the Lands jointly to the City and FrancoSud.
The Defendants cite Finlay v Canada, [1986] 2 SCR 607 in support of this proposition.
45 It is clear that the Community Association has no specific standing.
Accordingly, the next question is whether the Community Association satisfies the “public interest standing” threshold.
46 The law in Canada in respect of “public interest standing” has changed over the decades.
In recent years, the Courts have taken a more liberal approach to the concept.
While the Finlay decision relied upon by the Defendants is instructive, Canada (AG) v Downtown Eastside Sex Workers, 2012 SCC 45, [2012] 2 S.C.R.
524 is more relevant because it updates the law in this area.
47 In Downtown Eastside, Justice Cromwell commented that Canadian courts have relaxed limitations on public interest standing.

In particular, he commented that the Courts have taken a flexible, discretionary approach to public interest standing and are to be guided by the purposes which underlie the traditional limitations: Downtown Eastside, at para 1.

48 In analyzing the appropriate boundaries of “public interest standing”, Justice Cromwell commented at paras 35-36: The decision to grant or refuse standing involves the careful exercise of judicial discretion through the weighing of the three factors (serious justiciable issue, the nature of the plaintiff's interest, and other reasonable and effective means [of bringing the issue before the court]) … … the factors should be seen as interrelated considerations to be weighed cumulatively, not individually, and in light of their purposes.
49 The most significant shift that Downtown Eastside brought to the “public interest standing” framework was in respect of the third factor.
In his consideration of this factor, Justice Cromwell indicated that the question should be whether the proposed suit is a reasonable and effective means to bring the challenge to court.

He further indicated that this “… approach to the third factor better reflects the flexible, discretionary and purposive approach to public interest standing that underpins all of the Court's decisions in this area”: Downtown Eastside, at para 44.
50 The effect of that judicial comment was to make it clear that the strict requirement outlined by the majority in Minister of Justice v Borowski, [1981] 2 SCR 575 no longer applied.

In Borowski, the majority held at page 598 that the person seeking standing had “… to show … that there [was]…no other reasonable effective manner in which the issue may be brought before the Court” (emphasis added).

1. —Three Factors 51 Given this updated judicial framework, the facts must be considered in the context of these three enumerated factors to determine whether the Community Association should be granted “public interest standing”. a. —The First Factor—Serious Justiciable Issue 52 In Downtown Eastside at para 42, the Supreme Court confirmed its holding in Finlay that, to constitute a serious issue, a claim must be “far from frivolous”.

However, the courts need not examine the merits of the case in “other than a preliminary manner”. … b. —The Second Factor—The Nature of the Plaintiff's Interest 57 The second factor is “whether the party bringing the action has a real stake or a genuine interest in its outcome” (emphasis added): Downtown Eastside, at para 2.

The purpose underlying this factor “… reflects the concern for conserving scarce judicial resources …”: Downtown Eastside, at para 43, referencing Finlay at page 633. … c. —The Third Factor—Reasonable and Effective Means 64 Notwithstanding the above determination concerning the second factor, the Supreme Court of Canada's direction in Downtown Eastside is that all factors be considered cumulatively.
Accordingly, a review of the third factor is required.
65 The Community Association seeks relief under the Judicature Act, R.S.A.
2000, c.J-2 (the “Judicature Act”) and the Alberta Rules of Court, Alta.
Reg.
124/2010 (the “Rules of Court”).
It has chosen this procedure rather than seeking a judicial review or filing an objection under the MGA, which has a specific appeal provision.
66 This Court is not satisfied that the procedure chosen by the Community Association is the only “reasonable and effective means of bringing the issue[s] before the Court”.
Other appeal mechanisms were available, but were not pursued.
That being the case, the third factor has not been satisfied.
Party status?
In Auer v.
Auer, 2018 ABQB 510, 2018 CarswellAlta 1309, 73 Alta.
L.R.

744, the Attorney General of Canada applied for intervenor status in a matter in which one of the parties sought a declaration that the Federal Child Support Guidelines were ultra vires the Divorce Act (Canada).
Justice Gates granted that application, and then had to decide the extent to which the Attorney General would be allowed to participate in the action.
His Lordship granted what he termed “party-like status”.
Gates, J. said: 126 Rule 2.10 is silent on the scope of intervention that is appropriate when a court grants intervenor status pursuant to this rule.
Rule 2.10 does not specify whether this Court has the power to grant the Attorney General the status of a full party.

127 The Attorney General relies on the Ontario decision in North American Financial Group Inc v Ontario (Securities Commission), 2017 ONSC 2965, as support for the argument that she is entitled to party status.

However, in Stratum Projects Alberta Inc v Aman Building Corp, 2017 ABQB 351 at paras 21–28, Master Schlosser notes that the Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure, RRO 1990, Reg 194, explicitly allow for intervention as an added party, whereas the Alberta Rules of Court do not contain similarly explicit language.
As such, Master Schlosser questions whether Rule 2.10 contemplates granting party status to an intervenor.

128 Generally, Alberta case law cautions that the scope of any intervention should be limited to only what is required for a court to make a proper determination on the issues before it: R v Hirsekorn, 2011 ABQB 156 at para 21.
An intervenor should generally not be allowed to introduce new issues or enlarge the issues already before the court.

In the current circumstances, however, where this Court is faced with an otherwise unopposed challenge to the vires of the Guidelines, the Attorney General is, in my view, entitled to participate fully in this process.
129 Accordingly, the Attorney General of Canada is granted intervenor status with rights and duties comparable to that of a party, which includes:
(a) The right to cross-examine on the previously specified affidavits for no more than one day
(b) The right to make oral and/or written submissions on any aspect of the vires application, including evidentiary and jurisdictional issues
(c) The right to put public documents before the Court to establish legislative and social facts concerning the development and implementation of the Guidelines; and
(d) The right to appeal an adverse decision.

130 The Attorney General's right to appeal stems from the Alberta Rules of Court, which allows appeals from a party to an action heard before the Court of Queen's Bench: Peavine Metis Settlement v Whitehead, 2015 ABCA 366 at paras 50–52.
131 It is also applicable regardless of whether Rule 2.10 contemplates an intervenor being given party status.
Even if Rule 2.10 does not contemplate party status, I would still grant the Attorney General party-like status, including the right to appeal, due to the extraordinary nature of Dr.
Auer's otherwise unopposed vires challenge to the Guidelines.
Costs for Intervenors See the annotation “Costs for Intervenors” under Rule 10.31.
Generally see: Imperial Oil Ltd. v.
Alberta (Minister of Environment), 2005 ABCA 375, 2005 CarswellAlta 1595 at paragraph 25.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.11:1 Rule 2.11 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.11. 1. Lack of Capacity under R. 2.11(c) In Chutskoff Estate v. Bonora, 2013 ABQB 119, Madam Justice Ross said, at paragraph 19: 19 The Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act, whose definition of capacity is incorporated in Rule 2.11(c), provides that “an adult is presumed to have the capacity to make decisions until the contrary is determined”: s 2(a). It is in my view appropriate to take the same approach under Rule 2.11(c). The admitted fact that the Respondent suffers from a psychiatric condition does not mean that he lacks capacity as defined in Rule 2.11(c). Lack of capacity in the defined sense must be proved on a balance of probabilities. In Alberta (Public Guardian) v. C. (K.), 2015 ABQB 369, an application was brought under the Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act (Alberta) in relation to the guardianship of a 27 year old individual (DC) suffering from Down's Syndrome who lacked “the capacity to make informed decisions relating to such matters as health care; where, with whom and under what circumstances he will live; who he may associate with; participation in social activities; participation in educational, vocational and other training; employment; and the carrying on of any legal proceedings unrelated to financial matters. His judgment and insight were further impacted by a tobogganing accident in 2009 in which he sustained head injuries.” Justice Gates concluded that DC should be permitted to be represented by counsel for the limited purpose of putting forth his/her views on the application. Justice Gates said: 65 DC was represented by counsel throughout these proceedings. Counsel advised the Court that she had been retained to make submissions to the Court with regard to DC's views and wishes. She also indicated that he did not want to participate in the proceedings by way of giving evidence or through the cross examination of any witnesses. 66 DC's counsel relied on s. 28(1) of the AGTA, which directs the Court to consider “the views and wishes of the adult, if ascertainable.” 67 Rule 2.11 of the Alberta Rules of Court directs that a Represented Adult must have a litigation representative in order to bring, defend, continue or participate in an action. However, this rule is qualified by Rule 12.6(2), which provides that a child is not considered to be participating in an action for the purposes of the Rule 2.11 merely by being the subject of the dispute or being served with notice of the proceedings. 68 I accept the argument advanced by DC's counsel that Rule 12.6(2), by analogy, applies in these circumstances so as to obviate the requirement for DC to have a litigation representative appointed to permit him to participate in this action. Like a child, DC lacks the legal capacity to either represent himself or to retain counsel for that purpose. However, he clearly has an interest in these proceedings notwithstanding that he had no role in bringing, defending, or continuing them. His proposed participation in these proceedings is a very limited one—the opportunity to express his views and wishes prior to the rendering of a decision on this application. He does not wish to participate otherwise and, indeed, does not oppose his need of a guardian or, indeed, the Public Guardian's application in this instance. 69 In my view, DC should be permitted to be represented by counsel for this very limited purpose. I would note that counsel are frequently appointed in family law cases to “represent” the views and/or wishes of children relative to legal proceedings in which they are implicated. In such instances, this information can be very helpful to the Court in determining what is in the best interest of the child or children. The same principle should, by analogy, apply here, namely that the expression of DC's views and wishes will, potentially, be very helpful to the Court in determining what is in his best interest in the future. Accordingly, I find that Rule 2.11 does not preclude DC from being represented by counsel in these proceedings so as to allow his voice to be heard. 70 During the course of these proceedings, counsel for Mr. C took the position that DC lacked the capacity to retain or instruct counsel. While this legal issue was not fully argued before me, I would offer the view that I am inclined to agree with this position. However, it seems to me that counsel may reflect the views and wishes of either a child or, as in this instance, a represented adult, without having been formally retained or instructed so long as the child or represented adult has the necessary capacity to understand the nature of the proceedings, generally, and the ability or capacity to provide instruction with regard to his or her views relative to the proceeding. 2. Litigation representative for an estate In Kunkel v. Winquist, 2022 ABQB 367, 2022 CarswellAlta 1305, Justice Leonard said: [23] However, there is nothing in the language of the Rules of Court to suggest that the litigation representative of an estate must be a person who is entitled to apply for a grant of administration. There is also nothing in the case law to suggest that the possible litigation representatives for an estate should be limited to those people who are entitled to apply for a grant of administration. [24] Instead, when appointing a litigation representative, the primary goal of the Court is to ensure the interests of the estate are represented: Hughes Estate v Hughes, 2007 ABCA 277. Most importantly, a litigation representative should not be in conflict with the interests of the estate: Rufenak v Hope Mission, 2005 ABCA 129. The litigation representative should also be able to manage the litigation and be willing to pay the court costs of the litigation: see Rules of Court, r 10.47. [25] When it comes to the relationship between a litigation representative and an estate, a beneficiary of an estate can act as the litigation representative: Lux v Lux, 2021 ABCA 413 at para 5. However, this does not need to be the case: Gonnerud (Litigation Guardians of) v Gonnerud Estate, 2002 SCC 38 at para 21. Ultimately, the driving question for the Court is whether a litigation representative will represent the interests of the estate. [26] Considering these authorities, I conclude that it is not necessary for the litigation representative of an estate to have priority to apply for a grant of administration under the Estate Administration Act. …

2.11(c) In Chutskoff Estate v.

Bonora, 2013 ABQB 119, Madam Justice Ross said, at paragraph 19: 19 The Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act, whose definition of capacity is incorporated in Rule 2.11(c), provides that “an adult is presumed to have the capacity to make decisions until the contrary is determined”: s 2(a).
It is in my view appropriate to take the same approach under Rule 2.11(c).
The admitted fact that the Respondent suffers from a psychiatric condition does not mean that he lacks capacity as defined in Rule 2.11(c).
Lack of capacity in the defined sense must be proved on a balance of probabilities.
In Alberta (Public Guardian) v.
C.

(K.), 2015 ABQB 369, an application was brought under the Adult Guardianship and Trusteeship Act (Alberta) in relation to the guardianship of a 27 year old individual (DC) suffering from Down's Syndrome who lacked “the capacity to make informed decisions relating to such matters as health care; where, with whom and under what circumstances he will live; who he may associate with; participation in social activities; participation in educational, vocational and other training; employment; and the carrying on of any legal proceedings unrelated to financial matters.

His judgment and insight were further impacted by a tobogganing accident in 2009 in which he sustained head injuries.” Justice Gates concluded that DC should be permitted to be represented by counsel for the limited purpose of putting forth his/her views on the application.
Justice Gates said: 65 DC was represented by counsel throughout these proceedings.
Counsel advised the Court that she had been retained to make submissions to the Court with regard to DC's views and wishes.
She also indicated that he did not want to participate in the proceedings by way of giving evidence or through the cross examination of any witnesses.
66 DC's counsel relied on s.

28(1) of the AGTA, which directs the Court to consider “the views and wishes of the adult, if ascertainable.” 67 Rule 2.11 of the Alberta Rules of Court directs that a Represented Adult must have a litigation representative in order to bring, defend, continue or participate in an action.

However, this rule is qualified by Rule 12.6(2), which provides that a child is not considered to be participating in an action for the purposes of the Rule 2.11 merely by being the subject of the dispute or being served with notice of the proceedings.

68 I accept the argument advanced by DC's counsel that Rule 12.6(2), by analogy, applies in these circumstances so as to obviate the requirement for DC to have a litigation representative appointed to permit him to participate in this action.
Like a child, DC lacks the legal capacity to either represent himself or to retain counsel for that purpose.
However, he clearly has an interest in these proceedings notwithstanding that he had no role in bringing, defending, or continuing them.
His proposed participation in these proceedings is a very limited one—the opportunity to express his views and wishes prior to the rendering of a decision on this application.
He does not wish to participate otherwise and, indeed, does not oppose his need of a guardian or, indeed, the Public Guardian's application in this instance.
69 In my view, DC should be permitted to be represented by counsel for this very limited purpose.
I would note that counsel are frequently appointed in family law cases to “represent” the views and/or wishes of children relative to legal proceedings in which they are implicated.
In such instances, this information can be very helpful to the Court in determining what is in the best interest of the child or children.

The same principle should, by analogy, apply here, namely that the expression of DC's views and wishes will, potentially, be very helpful to the Court in determining what is in his best interest in the future.
Accordingly, I find that Rule 2.11 does not preclude DC from being represented by counsel in these proceedings so as to allow his voice to be heard.
70 During the course of these proceedings, counsel for Mr.
C took the position that DC lacked the capacity to retain or instruct counsel.
While this legal issue was not fully argued before me, I would offer the view that I am inclined to agree with this position.

However, it seems to me that counsel may reflect the views and wishes of either a child or, as in this instance, a represented adult, without having been formally retained or instructed so long as the child or represented adult has the necessary capacity to understand the nature of the proceedings, generally, and the ability or capacity to provide instruction with regard to his or her views relative to the proceeding.
Litigation representative for an estate In Kunkel v.

Winquist, 2022 ABQB 367, 2022 CarswellAlta 1305, Justice Leonard said: [23] However, there is nothing in the language of the Rules of Court to suggest that the litigation representative of an estate must be a person who is entitled to apply for a grant of administration.
There is also nothing in the case law to suggest that the possible litigation representatives for an estate should be limited to those people who are entitled to apply for a grant of administration.
[24] Instead, when appointing a litigation representative, the primary goal of the Court is to ensure the interests of the estate are represented: Hughes Estate v Hughes, 2007 ABCA 277.
Most importantly, a litigation representative should not be in conflict with the interests of the estate: Rufenak v Hope Mission, 2005 ABCA 129.
The litigation representative should also be able to manage the litigation and be willing to pay the court costs of the litigation: see Rules of Court, r 10.47.
[25] When it comes to the relationship between a litigation representative and an estate, a beneficiary of an estate can act as the litigation representative: Lux v Lux, 2021 ABCA 413 at para 5.
However, this does not need to be the case: Gonnerud (Litigation Guardians of) v Gonnerud Estate, 2002 SCC 38 at para 21.
Ultimately, the driving question for the Court is whether a litigation representative will represent the interests of the estate.

[26] Considering these authorities, I conclude that it is not necessary for the litigation representative of an estate to have priority to apply for a grant of administration under the Estate Administration Act. …

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.13 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.13:1 Rule 2.13 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.13. 1. Appointment by Instrument In Nahirney v. Ogilvie & Co., 2011 ABQB 586, 2011 CarswellAlta 2363, 525 A.R. 14, 26 C.P.C. (7th) 425, [2011] A.J. No. 1354, the Plaintiff's father sought to represent his daughter by virtue of a Power of Attorney executed by his daughter. Lee, J. said, at paragraphs 22–28: 22 Rule 2.13(e) allows a person to become an automatic litigation representative by virtue of having an instrument such as a power of attorney, However the Rule should only apply to instances in which a litigation representative is required to be appointed. If the result of Rule 2.13(e) was to allow anyone to appoint a non-lawyer as their de-facto representative in court, then s. 106 of the Legal Profession Act would be rendered meaningless. 23 The Alberta Rules of Court also contemplate a conflict with any other statutes in Rule 1.9, which reads: Conflicts and inconsistencies with enactments 1.9 Except as expressly provided, if there is a conflict or inconsistency between these rules and an enactment, the enactment prevails to the extent of the conflict or inconsistency. 24 Even if Mr. Nahirney is capable of being appointed litigation representative pursuant to the Alberta Rules of Court, he would still be prohibited from representing his daughter's interest in the litigation. The permissibility of litigation representatives to represent others in court has not been dealt with under the current Alberta Rules of Court. Our Court of Appeal has considered the use of Next Friends under the old Rules of Court in the case of a minor as follows: …[A] next friend is not a party to the lawsuit. He is an officer of the court under its control, and cannot even make a binding settlement on behalf of the infants (even as to modes of procedure). It is elementary that a non-lawyer cannot represent someone else as advocate before the superior courts. Salamon v. Alberta (Minister of Education) (1991), 120 AR 298 at para. 3. See also Torrance v. Alberta 2010 ABCA 88 at para. 14 Conclusion 25 Self represented litigants are expressly granted a right of audience before the court pursuant to Rule 2.22, … 26 The Plaintiff's father Mr. Nahirney is permitted to provide limited assistance to his daughter by virtue of Rule 2.23. … 27 Accordingly, the Ogilvie Defendants cannot object to Mr. Nahirney assisting his daughter pursuant to Rule 2.23. However Rule 2.23 does not permit Mr. Nahirney to stand in the place of a lawyer and represent his daughter. Rule 2.23 contains an explicit reference to s. 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act. The conduct of any person assisting a party before the Court must fall short of “acting as a barrister or solicitor” and “commencing, carrying on or defending an action or proceeding before a court or judge on behalf of another person”. 28 I conclude that Rule 2.11, 2.13 and 2.14(1) were intended to grant representation only in cases where a litigation representative was necessary under the Alberta Rules of Court. In the present case, the Plaintiff does not suffer from a disability and is not a minor, therefore there is no basis for the appointment of a Litigation Representative. In Champagne v. Sidorsky, 2012 ABQB 522, 2012 CarswellAlta 1437, 548 A.R. 10, Justice C. M. Jones noted at paragraph 5: 5 On November 17, 2011, Justice Hunt McDonald determined that Rule 2.13(e) should only apply in instances in which a litigation representative is required to be appointed. She determined that the appointment of Cindy and Cheri under the EPA did not automatically mean that Douglas was required or permitted to have a litigation representative.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.14 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) If an individual or estate who is required to have a litigation representative under rule 2.11 does not have one, an interested person (a) may file an affidavit in Form 1 containing the information described in subrule (2), and by doing so becomes the litigation representative for that individual or estate, and (b) where an interested person has, or proposes to, become the litigation representative under clause (a) for an estate, the interested person must serve notice of the appointment in Form 2 on the beneficiaries and heirs at law of the deceased. (2) The affidavit must include (a) the interested person's agreement in writing to be the litigation representative, (b) the reason for the self-appointment, (c) the relationship between the litigation representative and the individual or estate the litigation representative will represent, (d) a statement that the litigation representative has no interest in the action adverse in interest to the party the litigation representative will represent, (e) if the litigation representative is an individual, a statement that the litigation representative is a resident of Alberta, (f) if the litigation representative is a corporation, the place of business or activity of the corporation in Alberta, and (g) an acknowledgment of potential liability for payment of a costs award attributable to or liable to be paid by the litigation representative. (3) If a person proposes to become a self-appointed litigation representative for the estate of a deceased person, the affidavit referred to in subrule (2) must, in addition to the matters set out in subrule (2), disclose any of the following matters that apply: (a) whether the estate has a substantial interest in the action or proposed action; (b) whether the litigation representative has or may have duties to perform in the administration of the estate of the deceased; (c) whether an application has been or will be made for administration of the estate of the deceased; (d) whether the litigation representative does or may represent interests adverse to any other party in the action or proposed action. (e) [Repealed Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 2(b).] (4) A person proposing to become a self-appointed litigation representative has no authority to make or defend a claim or, without the Court's permission, to make an application or take any proceeding in an action, until the affidavit referred to in subrule (1)(a) is filed. Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 2

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.14:1 Rule 2.14 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.14. An Estate Requires Representation to Appear in Court In Oommen v. Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 34, 2015 CarswellAlta 102, 3 E.T.R. (4th) 207, Mr. Oommen, one of the named co-executors in a will not yet probated, “appointed himself the estate's litigation representative pursuant to Rule 2.14”, and now wished to represent (without counsel) the estate in the Court of Queen's Bench in relation to a judgment the deceased had obtained before his death. In an Application for Incidental Direction, Madam Justice Veldhuis held he could not do so without legal counsel. Her Ladyship said, at paragraphs 3-4: 3 The Rules of Court provide that individuals may represent themselves in an action: Rule 2.22. An estate is not an individual in this context but a separate legal entity. This has been established in the constitutional context: Stinson (Estate of) v British Columbia, 1999 BCCA 761 at para 15, 133 BCAC 15; Canada (Attorney General) v Hislop, 2007 SCC 10 at para 73, [2007] 1 SCR 429. In addition, Rule 2.14(1) refers to an “individual or estate” (emphasis added), indicating the two concepts are distinct. 4 An estate therefore requires representation to appear in court. Section 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act, RSA 2000, c L-8 provides that no person shall commence, carry on or defend an action or proceeding before a court or judge on another's behalf unless that person is an active member of the Law Society of Alberta. Section 106(2) provides a number of exceptions to this rule, none of which apply in the circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.16 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) This rule applies to an action concerning any of the following: (a) the administration of the estate of a deceased person; (b) property subject to a trust; (c) the interpretation of a written instrument; (d) the interpretation of an enactment. (2) In an action described in subrule (1), a person or class of persons who is or may be interested in or affected by a claim, whether presently or for a future, contingent or unascertained interest, must have a Court-appointed litigation representative to make a claim in or defend an action or to continue to participate in an action, or for a claim in an action to be made or an action to be continued against that person or class of persons, if the person or class of persons meets one or more of the following conditions: (a) the person, the class or a member of the class cannot be readily ascertained, or is not yet born; (b) the person, the class or a member of the class, though ascertained, cannot be found; (c) the person, the class or the members of the class can be ascertained and found, but the Court considers it expedient to make an appointment to save expense, having regard to all the circumstances, including the amount at stake and the degree of difficulty of the issue to be determined. (3) On application by an interested person, the Court may appoint a person as litigation representative for a person or class of persons to whom this rule applies on being satisfied that both the proposed appointee and the appointment are appropriate.

(1), a person or class of persons who is or may be interested in or affected by a claim, whether presently or for a future, contingent or unascertained interest, must have a Court-appointed litigation representative to make a claim in or defend an action or to continue to participate in an action, or for a claim in an action to be made or an action to be continued against that person or class of persons, if the person or class of persons meets one or more of the following conditions:
(a) the person, the class or a member of the class cannot be readily ascertained, or is not yet born
(b) the person, the class or a member of the class, though ascertained, cannot be found

(c) the person, the class or the members of the class can be ascertained and found, but the Court considers it expedient to make an appointment to save expense, having regard to all the circumstances, including the amount at stake and the degree of difficulty of the issue to be determined.

(3) On application by an interested person, the Court may appoint a person as litigation representative for a person or class of persons to whom this rule applies on being satisfied that both the proposed appointee and the appointment are appropriate.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.21:1 Rule 2.21 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.21. 1. Ordering Costs in Advance In 1985 Sawridge Trust v. Alberta (Public Trustee), 2013 ABCA 226, 553 A.R. 324, 2013 CarswellAlta 1015, the Trustees of the Sawridge Trust sought an order changing the designation of “beneficiaries” under the Trust. The learned Chambers judge noted that children who might be affected by the change were not represented by legal counsel, and in due course, over the opposition of the Trustees, the Public Trustee was appointed. The learned Chambers judge “also awarded advance costs to the Public Trustee on a solicitor and his own client basis, to be paid for by the Trust, and he exempted the Public Trustee from liability for any other costs of the litigation.” The Trustees appealed the order with respect to costs and the exemption. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, and held that the Chambers judge had jurisdiction to order advance costs, and said at paragraphs 23–26: 23 In our view, there are several sources of jurisdiction for an order of advance costs in the case before us. One is section 41 of the Public Trustee Act, SA 2004, c P-44.1 which provides: 41 Unless otherwise provided by an enactment, where the Public Trustee is a party to or participates in any matter before a court, (a) the costs payable to the Public Trustee, and the client, party or other person by whom the costs are to be paid, are in the discretion of the court, and (b) the court may order that costs payable to the Public Trustee are to be paid out of and are a charge on an estate. 24 It is evident that the court is vested with a large discretion with respect to an award of costs under section 41. While not dealing specifically with an award of advance costs, this discretionary power encompasses such an award. Further, the court has broad powers to “impose terms and conditions” upon the appointment of a litigation representative pursuant to Rule 2.21 … 25 The chambers judge also invoked parens patriae jurisdiction as enabling him to award advance costs, in the best interests of the children, to obtain the independent representation of the Public Trustee on their behalf. To the extent that there is any gap in statutory authority for the exercise of this power, the parens patriae jurisdiction is available. As this Court commented in Alberta (Child, Youth and Family Enhancement Act, Director) v. DL, 2012 ABCA 275, 536 AR 207, in situations where there is a gap in the legislative scheme, the exercise of the inherent parens patriae jurisdiction “is warranted whenever the best interests of the child are engaged” (para 4). 26 In short, a wide discretion is conferred with respect to the granting of costs under the Trustee Act, the terms of the appointment of a litigation representative pursuant to the Rules of Court, and in the exercise of parens patriae jurisdiction for the necessary protection of children. In our view, the discretion is sufficiently broad to encompass an award of advanced costs in the situation at hand.
