paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.22 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.22:1 Rule 2.22 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.22. 1. Rule Complements Legal Profession Act An individual has the right to commence and conduct ligitation on his own behalf. Section 103(2)(h) [of the Legal Profession Act] recognizes that right by excluding “a person who sues on his own behalf in an action, matter or proceeding to which he is a party” from the restrictions contained in s. 103(1). The Courts have traditionally accorded the right of audience to an individual appearing on his own behalf. Rule 5.3 confirms that practice and complements s. 103(2)(h). Professional Sign Crafters (1988) Ltd. v. Wedekind (1994), 19 Alta. L.R. (3d) 53 (Q.B.), at 59, per O'Leary, J. In Beacon Hill Service (2000) Ltd. v. Esso Petroleum Canada, 2011 ABQB 138, 2011 CarswellAlta 366, 512 A.R. 212, 45 Alta. L.R. (5th) 92, a lawyer was named personally as a defendant by counterclaim. An issue arose as to whether the lawyer had the right to represent himself in the litigation. At paragraphs 31–38, Macleod, J. said: 31 This leaves the question of whether Mr. Merchant has the right to represent himself. 32 The right to represent one's self has always been important and is enshrined in the Alberta Rules of Court, A.R. 124/2010. Our newly enacted Rule 2.22 provides that “Individuals may represent themselves in an action unless these rules otherwise provide.” Why should a person be deprived of this right simply because he is a lawyer? There is nothing in the Rules of Court that so provides. Could a lawyer simply say that in acting for himself, he is acting only in his capacity as a party and not as a barrister and solicitor? 33 Lawyers are not prohibited from being their own counsel as parties to a proceeding: Brogan v. Walker, 2001 NSSC 53, 193 N.S.R. (2d) 154 at para. 18. However, a lawyer's right of self-representation is not unqualified. Even when appearing on their own behalf, lawyers are still bound by the relevant codes of ethics and professional responsibility. A practicing lawyer who represents himself in a court of law is to conduct himself in a manner consistent with that expected of a member of the Law Society and with his status as an officer of the court gained from that membership: Parkridge Homes Ltd. v. Anglin, [1996] A.J. No. 768 (Alta. Q.B.) at paras. 32 and 33; Collins v. Collins, 1999 ABQB 707, 256 A.R. 311 at para. 26. 34 In Ritchot v. The Law Society of Manitoba, 2010 MBCA 13, 251 Man.R. (2d) 121, the Manitoba Court of Appeal at paras. 42–47 upheld the decision of the Law Society of Manitoba that Ritchot, a lawyer, was subject to the Manitoba Code of Professional Conduct notwithstanding that she was engaged in her own representation. In the result, the Court upheld the Law Society's finding that Ritchot was guilty of conduct unbecoming a lawyer. 35 The court's inherent jurisdiction to remove counsel, as well as the standard required to do so, was discussed by the Court in Everingham v Ont. (1992), 8 O.R. (3d) 121 (Gen. Div. [Div. Ct.]). In that case, there was no question of a conflict of interest. The facts were that a number of patients confined to a mental hospital applied for declarations that certain of their rights had been infringed. A Crown solicitor who was touring the hospital had a conversation with one of those patients in the absence of that patient's counsel. Though no confidential information was obtained in that conversation, the Court held that it was necessary to remove the solicitor. The Court held as follows at paras. 27–29: It is within the inherent jurisdiction of a superior court to deny the right of audience to counsel when the interests of justice so require by reason of conflict or otherwise. This power does not depend on the rules of professional conduct made by the legal profession and is not limited to cases where the rules are breached. The issue here is not whether or not the rule was breached or whether the solicitor worked for the government. Nor is it solely whether the patient lost confidence in the process. The issue is whether a fair-minded reasonably informed member of the public would conclude that the proper administration of justice required the removal of the solicitor. [Emphasis added.] 36 It seems reasonable to conclude that circumstances could arise where a lawyer's breach of professional ethics would cause a fair-minded, reasonably informed member of the public to conclude that the proper administration of justice required the removal of the solicitor, even in a case where that solicitor represented only himself. Those who have been entrusted with the title of lawyer, barrister or solicitor, and the powers thereof should not be allowed to ignore their duties as officers of the court simply because they are self-represented litigants. 37 This raises the somewhat thorny question of how that removal would be effected. Clearly, the question is substantially simpler when parties and counsel are separate individuals. If counsel is removed, the party may choose to obtain replacement counsel or to represent himself. But how is a solicitor who is himself the party to be removed? The Court in Everingham refers to denying the right of audience. The court, as part of its inherent right to control its own process, may deny the right of audience, that is, the right to be heard, to a self-represented solicitor when, to return to the phraseology in Forward, “the preservation of the integrity of the system of justice” so requires. In light of my decision below, I need not determine how this would be carried out in practice. 38 Based on the above, it is clear the starting point is that Mr. Merchant does have a right to represent himself. However, he is bound by the Law Society of Alberta's Code of Professional Conduct. In the end, Justice Macleod permitted the lawyer to represent himself but added this warning (at paragraph 40): 40 However, I want to make it clear that this circumstance is subject to re-evaluation if and when necessary. Although certainly I question the wisdom of Mr. Merchant representing himself, I have not been presented with evidence to justify denying him this right at this time. However, if such evidence is forthcoming as this matter unfolds, it will be duly considered and the question re-evaluated. The appeal from Justice McLeod's decision was dismissed: Beacon Hill Service (2000) Ltd. v. Esso Petroleum Canada, 2012 ABCA 269, 2012 CarswellAlta 1563, 536 A.R. 221, 70 Alta. L.R. (5th) 238. 2. An Estate is Not an Individual In Chapman Estate v. Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 34, 2015 CarswellAlta 102, 3 E.T.R. (4th) 207, Madam Justice Veldhuis said, at paragraphs 3-4: 3 The Rules of Court provide that individuals may represent themselves in an action: Rule 2.22. An estate is not an individual in this context but a separate legal entity. This has been established in the constitutional context: Stinson (Estate of) v British Columbia, 1999 BCCA 761 at para 15, 133 BCAC 15; Canada (Attorney General) v Hislop, 2007 SCC 10 at para 73, [2007] 1 SCR 429. In addition, Rule 2.14(1) refers to an “individual or estate” (emphasis added), indicating the two concepts are distinct. 4 An estate therefore requires representation to appear in court. Section 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act, RSA 2000, c L-8 provides that no person shall commence, carry on or defend an action or proceeding before a court or judge on another's behalf unless that person is an active member of the Law Society of Alberta. Section 106(2) provides a number of exceptions to this rule, none of which apply in the circumstances of this case. 3. Corporations Must Be Represented by Lawyers In 908077 Alberta Ltd. v. 1313608 Alberta Ltd., 2015 ABCA 117, Justice Slatter said: 2 Rule 2.22 provides that an “individual” may be self-represented in the superior courts. The statutory and case law confirms that other types of litigants in civil cases, including corporations, must be represented by a lawyer: Lameman v Alberta, 2012 ABCA 59 at paras. 9, 35, 522 AR 140; Chapman Estate v Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 34 at paras. 3-4; Legal Profession Act, RSA 2000, c. L-8, s. 106. 3 It follows that the corporate appellant must retain counsel to represent it in this appeal. There are several advantages to doing business through a corporation (such as limited liability, and perpetual succession) but also some burdens. Using a lawyer during litigation is one such burden. If the corporate appellant is able, in this appeal, to establish some right to be represented by its non-lawyer directors, then it could continue to pursue the landlord and tenant dispute itself. However, as the law presently stands, the appellant must have counsel for this appeal. In the Queen's Bench ruling (2015 ABQB 108) which the Court of Appeal was reviewing, Associate Chief Justice Rooke said: 56 In summary: 1. an individual may represent themselves in the Alberta Court of Queen's Bench; 2. an estate, corporation, or litigation representative must be represented in the Alberta Court of Queen's Bench by a person authorized to practice law under the Legal Profession Act; 3. any common law or inherent discretion to permit representation in the Alberta Court of Queen's Bench by a non-lawyer has been extinguished by the New Rules; 4. New Rule 2.23 allows any person to provide only silent and passive support in court, provided those activities are restricted to a “McKenzie Friend” role; and 5. Professional Sign Crafters (1988) Ltd. v Wedekind, Pacer Enterprises Ltd. v Cummings, and Balogun v Pandher are no longer good law in relation to the right to physically appear in court as a representative and have been overruled by Lameman v Alberta (C.A.). The Court of Appeal made no adverse comment about that summary, and in Landmass Dirtworx Ltd. v. Prairie Mountain Construction (2010) Inc., 2015 ABQB 362, Justice Graesser said that A.C.J. Rooke's “decision was essentially upheld by the Court of Appeal”. Justice Graesser went on to say (at paragraph 17 of Landmass: 17 While the 908077 decision in the Court of Appeal is from one Court of Appeal judge and not from a full panel, to the extent that it may not be binding law in Alberta, the reasons expressed by Rooke ACJ and by Slattter JA are compelling and I will follow them. For an example of the decision in 908077 Alberta Ltd. v. 1313608 Alberta Ltd., 2015 ABCA 117, being applied, see: R. Floden Services Ltd. v. Solomon, 2015 ABQB 450 at paragraphs 12–14. 908077 Alberta Ltd. v. 1313608 Alberta Ltd. was applied in Park Avenue Flooring Inc. v. EllisDon Construction Services Inc., 2016 ABCA 211, 2016 CarswellAlta 1251 at paragraph 8. In Real Estate Strategies Group Inc. v. Prairie Communities Corp., 2016 ABCA 286, 2016 CarswellAlta 1831, Madam Justice Paperny said: 4 As noted, Mr. Penner seeks an order permitting him to represent RESG in court. He is not a lawyer. The current law in Alberta is well settled: this Court does not have the discretion to allow a non- lawyer to represent a party in Court: see Lameman v Alberta, 2012 ABCA 59, 348 DLR (4th) 45 [Lameman]; 908077 Alberta Ltd (Escape & Relax) v 1313608 Alberta Ltd, 2015 ABCA 117, [2015] 8 WWR 310; Park Avenue Flooring Inc v EllisDon Construction Services Inc, 2016 ABCA 211, [2016] AWLD 3576. 5 The Legal Professions Act, RSA 2000, c L-8, ss 102(2) and 106, governs who may appear before the courts [sections of the legislation omitted]. 6 Lameman clearly held that appearing in court and giving argument or leading evidence on behalf of one of the parties falls within the meaning of s 106 (1)(b) of the Legal Professions Act as acting as a barrister or solicitor: para 13. Logically, this principle extends to the bringing of court applications on behalf of those parties. 7 Rule 2.22 of the Rules of Court provides that only individuals can be self-represented. Corporations are not individuals and cannot represent themselves in court. 8 Rule 2.23(1) allows someone to provide assistance to a party. However, that assistance does not include speaking for the party, and is expressly limited to that which does not contravene s 106(1) of the Legal Professions Act. 9 Bringing court applications on behalf of a party falls directly under section 106(1)(c) of the Legal Professions Act. In Pacer Enterprises Ltd v Cummings, 2004 ABCA 28 at para 14, 346 AR 161, this Court concluded that the “right of audience” conferred on an agent either by statute or the then Rules of Court, Alta Reg 390/1968, r 5.4 (now succeeded by Rule 2.22(1)) does not include the right to prepare or file documents in furtherance of litigation. These acts can only be performed by members of the legal profession. See Allen Qui Tam v Jarvis (1871), 32 UCR 56, 32 UCQB 56 (Upper Canada QB), and R v Nicholson (1979), 14 AR 450, 96 DLR (3d) 693 (CA). 10 The case law and the Legal Professions Act make it clear that a corporation must be represented at the Court of Queen's Bench and the Court of Appeal by a person authorized to practice law under the Legal Professions Act and that the court has no common law or inherent discretion to permit such representation unless otherwise provided for. Any residual discretion has been extinguished by the new Rules of Court. 11 The argument raised by RESG relies on comments from the rules committee that preceded the enactment of the new Rules of Court and cannot be sustained. Moreover, Mr. Penner argues that the natural person powers granted corporations under the Business Corporations Act, RSA 2000, c B-9, should prevail over the Legal Professions Act. The court in Whitbread v Walley (1988), 26 BCLR (2d) 203, 51 DLR (4th) 509 (CA) held that section 7 of the Charter is not infringed in these circumstances. Section 7 of the Charter is not a guarantee of financial prosperity or economic security. Also see Vysek v Nova Gas International Ltd, 2002 ABCA 112 at para 13, 303 AR 209. In National Leasing Group Inc. v. Acme Enterprises Ltd., 2015 ABQB 631 (Master), Master Schlosser made some very thoughtful comments about the position in which closely-held corporations find themselves if they cannot afford to hire a lawyer. The learned Master said: 5 The second issue regarding “representation” is somewhat more complicated given that section 106 of the Legal Profession Act, prohibits non-lawyers representing individuals, or companies, even with their proxy. The old Rules (R 5.4, AR 390/1968) provided a discretionary exception but the 908 case confirms that this is no more.2 6 This case has some features that distinguish it from the 908 and the Landmass decisions. In 908, two directors (with resolutions purporting to authorize them to represent the company) sought to make an application on its behalf. An untrained director may have no grasp of the relevant tests or legal issues. However, broadly stated, the central issue in that context appears to be whether third parties would suffer as a result of not lifting the veil. 23 Kosmopoulos, Elbow and the root case cited by Elbow; Transamerica Life Insurance Co. of Canada v Canada Life Assurance Co. (1996) 28 OR (3d) 423, (Ont SC) are about the use of (usually) closely-held companies to throw up obstacles in the path of justice. Nor does it extend to authorizing a breach of statute, or sanctioning an offence: Lameman v Alberta, 2012 ABCA 59 at paras 35–37 and Scotia Mortgage Corporation v Gutierrez, 2012 ABQB 683, per Laycock, M.
(and see 908, especially para.
37 et seq, and the cases cited there).
Separate Legal Personality 18 Incorporation usually gives a number of advantages; the central one usually being the limited exposure of the owners of the company to liability.
This is the “corporate entity doctrine” found in Salomon v Salomon and Company Ltd, [1887] AC 22 (HL); Soper v Little John (1901) 31 SCR 572.
There are other advantages, but that is usually the main one.
The burdens of incorporation (such as having to have a lawyer represent the company) usually follow the benefits, (and see Kosmopoulos, below, esp at p.

19 In Elbow River Marketing Limited Partnership v Canada Clean Funds Inc., 2012 ABCA 328, our Court of Appeal observed: Canadian Courts will pierce the corporate veil only when a corporation has been completely dominated and controlled and used as a shield for fraudulent or improper conduct.
20 Elbow was a summary judgment case.
In that case, the court decided that there was a triable issue (on the old test) and that the case should proceed to trial.
21 With respect, this observation is somewhat narrower than that of Wilson J., speaking for the majority in Kosmopoulos v Constitution Insurance Company, 1987, 1 SCR 2 at 1012.
She observed that the law in that area had (then) not followed any consistent principle, but, cited the English Company Law Textbook: Modern Company Law, LCB Gover, 4th ed, 1979 at p.
112, and said that the corporate entity doctrine would not be enforced if the result was “to flagrantly opposed to justice, convenience or the interest of the revenue”.
22 A central or unifying principle about when the separate legal personality of the company may be ignored has proved elusive.
Much of the discussion is dicta.
Often times a result can be explained or justified on other principles.
However, broadly stated, the central issue in that context appears to be whether third parties would suffer as a result of not lifting the veil.
23 Kosmopoulos, Elbow and the root case cited by Elbow; Transamerica Life Insurance Co. of Canada v Canada Life Assurance Co.
(1996) 28 OR (3d) 423, (Ont SC) are about the use of (usually) closely-held companies to throw up obstacles in the path of justice.
I am not aware of any cases that would prevent another use; to ignore separate legal personality to remove obstacles, and permit access to justice.
24 Prest v Petrodell Resources Limited[2013] 2 AC 415 (United Kingdon Supreme Court) contains a helpful recent review of this area of the law.
Lord Sumpton, in an attempt to reconcile the many conflicting and competing authorities, identified central themes of “concealment” and “evasion”.

The evasion principle allows the court to “disregard the corporate veil if there is a legal right against the person in control of it which exists independently of the company's involvement and that a company is interposed so that the separate legal personality of the company will defeat the right or frustrate its enforcement”.
(Prest, para.

28) (emphasis added) 25 In some cases the principal of a closely held company wishes to use a company as a shield; accepting the benefits of incorporation but not a particular burden such as the burden imposed by section 106 of the Legal Profession Act.
And when the company and the principals are named together, there is typically a conflict when the owner seeks to evade liability by passing it all to the company.

In those circumstances, there would be an obvious conflict in letting the individual speak for the company, unless liability is joint. “No Benefit No Burden” 26 Drawing aside the corporate veil may be a way to deal with the problem of representation in the current statutory regime.
If an owner wishes to step up for a limited company because it has no other means of speaking, he could be offered the opportunity to step out from behind it.
This would be consistent with the benefits and burdens test that is central to the analysis: In Kosmopoulos it was expressed to be “not blowing hot and cold at the same time” (p.
In Prest (at para.
35), it was acknowledged that the veil was sometimes lifted to deprive the company or its owner of an advantage.
27 Doing this would mean ignoring the separate legal personality of the company by treating it, for the purposes of the lawsuit, as if the company were a firm.
It may mean adjusting the parties.
I acknowledge this would not work so well for anything other than the so-called “one-man companies”; or when the corporate party is a Plaintiff.
However, it may provide a way to deal with the problem of representation that does not require adjournment or default.
But this is for another day or another case.
It is unnecessary here.
Options 28 It seems that the options available to the court in this legislative regime are: 1.
To hear the officer's account of what the lawsuit is about (which is not evidence of any kind), to help the court decide what the next step should be.
This provides a limited right of audience, falling short of representation as that term is used in the Legal Profession Act.
To review the affidavit evidence on the file to see whether a fair and just determination of the issues is possible based on the evidence on file.
If necessary, to adjourn the matter on terms; such as requiring the litigant to retain counsel, or risk losing the lawsuit for nonappearance.

To hear the evidence and the representations of the individual in their own right and, if appropriate, to apply it to the company if there is a unity in their position; such as where their liability is joint.
In appropriate circumstances, to disregard the separate legal personality of the corporate party.

This may require giving the company owner the option as being added as a party, or, if she is already a party, to hear representations on the condition that the liability of the corporate defendant and the individual defendant will be joint and several.
They would stand or fall together, which would eliminate any conflict or evasion.
This last approach is not likely to be necessary if the owner is already named individually and the liability sought against the owner and the corporate entity is joint, as is the case here.
In a manner of speaking this situation involves treating the individual's position as representative because the corporate distinction in these circumstances is an empty fiction.
29 As it turns out, there is no real question about the company's liability on the facts of this case.
The only real issue is the exposure of the individual defendants who, if they are liable under the agreement, are liable jointly and severally.

30 In the circumstances I am going to consider the evidence on file and the representations of Paul Hedges, at least in his own right, rather than to adjourn this application further for representation or, (and without more,) simply to give judgment against Angela, Christopher and Acme for non-appearance.
The Summary Judgment application has been adjourned several times already.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.23 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) The Court may permit a person to assist a party before the Court in any manner and on any terms and conditions the Court considers appropriate. (2) Without limiting subrule (1), assistance may take the form of (a) quiet suggestions, (b) note-taking, (c) support, or (d) addressing the particular needs of a party. (3) Despite subrule (1), no assistance may be permitted (a) that would contravene section 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act, (b) if the assistance would or might be disruptive, or (c) if the assistance would not meet the purpose and intention of these rules. (4) This rule does not affect the discretion of the Court, subject to any limits imposed under the Legal Profession Act, to grant a right of audience to any agent, other than a lawyer, to speak on behalf of an individual or corporation. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.23:1 Rule 2.23 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.23. 1. Inherent Jurisdiction In MD v. Alberta (Director of Child and Family Services), 2024 ABKB 565, Justice Feasby discussed the Court's inherent jurisdiction to permit laypersons to act as litigation representatives. Justice Feasby said: [15] The Legal Profession Act, RSA 2000, c L-8 s 106 provides that no person other than a lawyer who is a member of the Law Society of Alberta shall “act as a barrister or solicitor in any court of civil or criminal jurisdiction.” There are two exceptions to this prohibition. First, lawyers from most other provinces may appear in Alberta courts on a temporary basis pursuant to the National Mobility Agreement. Second, courts have the inherent jurisdiction to permit laypersons to act as litigation representatives: R v Dick, 2002 BCCA 27 at para 6 and 1985 Sawridge Trust v Alberta (Public Trustee), 2017 ABQB 530 at para 55. This latter exception is subject to limits and does not permit the proposed representative engage in the practice of law: Pacer Enterprises Ltd. v Cummings, 2004 ABCA 28 at para 14. [16] The discretion to allow a layperson to act as a litigation representative should be exercised “rarely and with caution”: R v Dick, at para 6 quoting B.C. Telephone Co. v Rueben, 1982 CanLII 588 (BC SC), [1982] 5 WWR 428 (BCSC) at 434. Rule 2.23(2) specifies the type of assistance that may be given by a lay representative: (a) quiet suggestions, (b) note-taking, (c) support, or (d) addressing the particular needs of a party. [17] Rule 2.23(3) provides that no assistance may be permitted: (a) that would contravene section 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act, (b) if the assistance would or might be disruptive, or (c) if the assistance would not meet the purpose and intention of these rules. [18] A court must consider whether the proposed litigation representative's presence is necessary for the unrepresented litigant to have a fair hearing and evaluate the risk that the litigation representative poses to the court process. A potential litigation representative who has a track record of using pseudo-legal arguments is not an appropriate litigation representative: Bonville v President's Choice Financial, 2024 ABKB 483 at para 88. 2. Right of Audience In Lameman v. Alberta, 2011 ABQB 396, 2011 CarswellAlta 2287, 521 A.R. 99; affirmed 2012 ABCA 59, 2012 CarswellAlta 355, 522 A.R. 140, 348 D.L.R. (4th) 45, Justice Yamauchi had before him an application for a right of audience to be granted to certain British barristers (“the Tooks barristers”) so that they might assist the Plaintiffs in their action against the Defendants. The Tooks barristers were not members of the Law Society of Alberta. In ruling that he would not grant a right of audience to the Tooks barristers, his Lordship said, at paragraphs 34–39, 41: 34 The Alberta Court of Appeal in Pacer Enterprises, held that whether a non-lawyer is practising law is a question of degree. As mentioned earlier, no one takes issue with Tooks barristers providing support to Woodco through research and drafting, provided Woodco, as counsel of record, assumes ultimate responsibility for the work product. 35 Beyond this area of consensus, there was little agreement. Significant time was spent in oral argument on what constitutes the “practice of law.” It is not the task of this Court to delineate the limits of the practice of law; nor would it be desirable so to do. The law, as a profession, evolves along with societal needs and desires. 36 However, we are dealing here with represented Plaintiffs proposing to engage trained foreign lawyers who are non-members. This Court finds that the proposed involvement of Tooks barristers, including questioning of witnesses, preparation of argument, and advocacy before the Court, clearly encompasses matters in respect of which law students receive training and which the public understands to form part of a litigator's stock and trade. It involves acts which in the usual course, if performed improperly, might appropriately draw comment or sanction from the Law Society. If these tasks do not form part of the practice of law, what does? 37 The Alberta Legislature has chosen to grant the privilege of self-regulation to the legal profession in Alberta. The Alberta Legislature enacted LPA s. 106(1) for the purpose of ensuring, among other things, that lawyers practising in Alberta be competent and proficient, adequately insured by the Alberta Lawyers' Insurance Association, and bound by the CPC. While Tooks barristers may well be competent and proficient, there was no evidence before this Court that they are insured, nor did the Plaintiffs present evidence to establish that Tooks barristers would be bound by the CPC. 38 The Plaintiffs rely heavily on Professional Signcrafters. That decision addressed Old Rules r. 5.4. It is noteworthy that the issue before O'Leary J., as he then was, was whether the director of the plaintiff corporation had contravened the LPA by commencing an action on behalf of the plaintiff corporation. The director had already lost on an appeal of a Master's decision denying him standing to make representations on behalf of the plaintiffs at the hearing of the motion to strike out the plaintiffs' pleadings. Although O'Leary J. in obiter dictum distinguished between the right of audience in Old Rules r. 5.4, and the right to practice law under the equivalent of LPA s. 106(1), there is no suggestion that he intended his comments to extend so as to allow trained lawyers to circumvent the regime of self-regulation established by the Alberta Legislature, particularly where the party seeking this relief is already represented by counsel of record. 39 Further, New Rules r. 2.23 speaks not of “represent” and “representation,” but of “assist” and “assistance.” While the list of forms of assistance set forth in New Rules r. 2.23(2) is not exhaustive, New Rules r. 2.23(3) is absolutely clear that, despite the apparent broadness of New Rules r. 2.23(1), a court has no discretion to permit assistance where the court's ruling would contravene LPA s. 106(1). This Court has no inherent jurisdiction to make an order negating the unambiguous expression of the will of the Alberta Legislature: Baxter Student Housing Ltd. v. College Housing Co-Operative Ltd., [1976] 2 S.C.R. 475 at 480. If this language left any room for doubt, the Information Note that one finds in the New Rules emphasizes that the “assistance” must fall short of “acting as a barrister or solicitor.” This Court need not determine the broadness (or narrowness) of New Rules r. 2.23. In particular, it need not determine whether New Rules r. 2.23 is or is not limited to self-represented litigants by virtue of the fact that New Rules r. 2.22 is headed “Self-represented litigants,” New Rules r. 2.23 is headed “Assistance before the Court,” and there is no mention of self-represented litigants in the title of the division of the New Rules in which New Rules r. 2.23 appears. … 41 This Court finds that the LPA and New Rules r. 2.23 prohibit Tooks barristers' proposed expanded participation in these proceedings and, in particular, in the Applications to Strike. The LPA and New Rules r. 2.23 do not provide an alternative basis for this participation. In the Court of Appeal (Lameman v. Alberta, 2012 ABCA 59, 2012 CarswellAlta 355, 522 A.R. 140, 348 D.L.R. (4th) 45), Justice Côté said, at paragraphs 25–27: 25 It might be objected that I am distorting the argument of the appellant, and that he does not call for an unregulated situation. He relies on R 2.23, which says that “The Court may permit a person to assist a party before the Court …”. If that is the suggestion, it seems to me at best to embrace a new system far feebler than the present system. Could a judge screen who appears? Would it be desirable to bypass the entire elaborate screening and evaluation system by Canada's various law societies and national accreditation bodies, set up by or under legislation, and instead hand that accrediting and disciplinary work to an individual chambers judge with no administrative assistance or records, nor training in this specialized field? Surely not. And it is clearly not the policy of the Legislature. 26 Besides, relying on individual judges to screen misses a bigger point. If there is an exception to s 106 of the Legal Profession Act, then no screening may be possible. There may be nothing to stop anyone at all from walking into a courtroom and acting as the advocate for one of the parties. Nothing in the Rules of Court directly or independently bars non-lawyers from acting as advocates (or otherwise practising law). It is only the Legal Profession Act which does that. Rule 2.23(1) lets the Court permit a non-party non-lawyer to assist a party. But if no such request is made, the Court may have no role to play, if s 106 of the Legal Profession Act truly does not apply. If the appellant's argument were right, maybe the unqualified person could appear as an advocate as of right, no matter what the judge said or thought. So what the appellant argues here would prove too much. 27 On the other hand, if the court has an inherent power to give an unqualified person audience, maybe the court has inherent power to exclude unqualified persons acting as advocates. But that question arises only because of the postulated hole in s 106. To invent a hole in an unqualified prohibition in a public statute, just to invoke a supposed ancient and inherent power in someone else partly to plug that hole, would be very roundabout. That is like postulating that the Legislature had deliberately built a dyke against the sea with a hole in it, because they knew that a little boy might come along and stick his finger in the hole. 3. Consequences of Violating Legal Professions Act In Professional Sign Crafters (1988) Ltd. v. Wedekind, 1994 CarswellAlta 90, 153 A.R. 358, 19 Alta. L.R. (3d) 53, 24 C.P.C. (3d) 387 (Q.B.), the statement of claim of the corporate plaintiff was prepared and issued by David Stanley, the sole director and officer of the plaintiffs. When considering the consequences of corporations violating the Legal Professions Act regarding the commencement of an action, O'Leary J. said at pp. 63-64: Section 103(1) of the Act forbids the commencement of an action in the Court of Queen's Bench by an individual who is not a member of the Law Society. Subsection (2) exempts certain individuals and circumstances from that prohibition. A corporation cannot act “in person” within subs. (2)(h) and no other exemption applies. A corporation is a legal entity separate from its shareholders, directors, officers and employees and none of them can commence an action on behalf of the corporation without contravening s. 103. I agree with the Master's conclusion that Stanley violated the Act when he prepared, issued and served the Statement of Claim on behalf of the Plaintiffs … The purpose of the Act is to protect the public by preventing unqualified individuals from practicing law. Those who contravene the Act are subject to penalties. There is nothing express or implied in the statute imposing any sanctions on those for whom unqualified individuals purport to act. In many cases the “clients” will be ignorant of the lack of qualifications and it would be harsh to strike out their actions as nullities. I cannot imagine a valid reason for doing so … In my opinion, there is no justification in principle or practice for declaring the action a nullity. The Court has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject-matter. It is not suggested that the Statement of Claim is defective in form or that it does not disclose a cause of action. The Defendants have suffered no prejudice which cannot be remedied in costs. There is no policy reason for declaring the action a nullity. The provisions of the Act can be enforced against those who contravene its terms without the necessity of striking out the underlying proceedings. In my opinion the proper disposition of this application is to direct a stay of the action until such time as the Plaintiffs are represented on the record by a qualified agent as required by the Act and the Rules of Court. 4. The Rule Does Not Permit Violation of the Legal Profession Act In Chapman Estate v. Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 58, 2015 CarswellAlta 187, 3 E.T.R. (4th) 211, an individual was the co-executor of an estate which had as one of its assets a judgment obtained by Mr. Chapman prior to his death. The co-executor was not permitted to appear in Court to represent the estate in judgment enforcement proceedings. Madam Justice Veldhuis said, at paragraphs 2–4: 2 Mr. Oommen appeared before several justices of the Court of Queen's Bench without incident. However, at one appearance before Michalyshyn J, Mr. Oommen was told that the Legal Profession Act, RSA 2000, c L-8 prevented him from appearing in court on behalf of the estate. The Court issued an order to that effect which also dismissed Mr. Oommen's substantive application to review a garnishment order. Mr. Oommen appealed that order, and appeared before me in chambers seeking the right to appear on behalf of the estate in the Court of Appeal. I dismissed his application: Oommen v Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 34. Mr. Oommen is now applying for permission to appeal my decision to a panel of this Court. 3 It is unfortunate that Mr. Oommen was permitted to appear in the Court of Queen's Bench on several occasions prior to being told that he could not represent the Chapman estate. The Legal Profession Act does not permit Mr. Oommen, either as a co-executor, co-beneficiary, personal representative or litigation representative to appear in court on behalf of the estate of Mr. Chapman. This action can only proceed through the courts if the estate is represented by someone authorized to appear for others in accordance with the Legal Profession Act. Mr. Oommen is not one of these people. There is also no authority in the Survival of Actions Act, RSA 2000, c S-27, for the proposition that Mr. Oommen can act for the estate in court. That Act only establishes that a cause of action survives for the benefit of an estate, and allows for the appointment of a litigation representative. It says nothing of who can appear in court for an estate. 4 Rule 2.23 of the Rules of Court allows a court to grant permission to a person to assist a litigant, but this appointment cannot conflict with s 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act. The law is clear that Mr. Oommen cannot act for this estate in court. There are many reasons why only those licenced to practice law may appear on behalf of others (amongst them the fact that lawyers are professionally trained, and insured against negligence for the benefit of clients). These are sound policy reasons that support the legislative framework. 5. Discretion to grant right of audience to non-lawyer In Vuong Van Tai Holding v. Alberta (Minister of Justice and Solicitor General), 2020 ABCA 169, 2020 CarswellAlta 793, Justice Slatter noted the effect of the 2020 amendment to the rule: [15] Rule 2.23(4) of the Rules of Court has now restored the discretion of the Court to allow a right of audience to a non-lawyer: see Pacer Enterprises Ltd v Cummings, 2004 ABCA 28 at para. 8, 26 Alta LR (4th) 241, 346 AR 161, citing Professional Sign Crafters (1988) Ltd. v Wedekind (1994), 1994 CanLII 9245 (AB QB), 19 Alta LR (3d) 53 at pp. 57-8, 153 AR 358: In order to place the issues in perspective it is important to distinguish between the inherent discretion of a superior Court to permit a non-lawyer to appear physically in Court or before a judge as a representative or advocate of another person (the “right of audience”), and the right of an individual to represent another person in respect of legal matters generally, that is, the right to practice law The Court now has a discretion to permit an individual to speak in court on behalf of a corporation. Clause 5 of the order of October 8, 2015 is accordingly rescinded. To be clear, the enactment of R. 2.23(4) does not mean that non-lawyers have an unlimited right to represent corporations. The presumption is still that corporations must be represented by lawyers. Rule 2.23(4) merely restores the discretion of judges to give a right of audience in court to non-lawyers connected to the corporation: Pacer Enterprises at para. 13.

2.23 is headed “Assistance before the Court,” and there is no mention of self-represented litigants in the title of the division of the New Rules in which New Rules r.
2.23 appears. … 41 This Court finds that the LPA and New Rules r.
2.23 prohibit Tooks barristers' proposed expanded participation in these proceedings and, in particular, in the Applications to Strike.
The LPA and New Rules r.
2.23 do not provide an alternative basis for this participation.
In the Court of Appeal (Lameman v.
Alberta, 2012 ABCA 59, 2012 CarswellAlta 355, 522 A.R.
(4th) 45), Justice Côté said, at paragraphs 25–27: 25 It might be objected that I am distorting the argument of the appellant, and that he does not call for an unregulated situation.
He relies on R 2.23, which says that “The Court may permit a person to assist a party before the Court …”.
If that is the suggestion, it seems to me at best to embrace a new system far feebler than the present system.
Could a judge screen who appears?

Would it be desirable to bypass the entire elaborate screening and evaluation system by Canada's various law societies and national accreditation bodies, set up by or under legislation, and instead hand that accrediting and disciplinary work to an individual chambers judge with no administrative assistance or records, nor training in this specialized field?
Surely not.
And it is clearly not the policy of the Legislature.
26 Besides, relying on individual judges to screen misses a bigger point.
If there is an exception to s 106 of the Legal Profession Act, then no screening may be possible.
There may be nothing to stop anyone at all from walking into a courtroom and acting as the advocate for one of the parties.
Nothing in the Rules of Court directly or independently bars non-lawyers from acting as advocates (or otherwise practising law).
It is only the Legal Profession Act which does that.
Rule 2.23(1) lets the Court permit a non-party non-lawyer to assist a party.
But if no such request is made, the Court may have no role to play, if s 106 of the Legal Profession Act truly does not apply.
If the appellant's argument were right, maybe the unqualified person could appear as an advocate as of right, no matter what the judge said or thought.
So what the appellant argues here would prove too much.
27 On the other hand, if the court has an inherent power to give an unqualified person audience, maybe the court has inherent power to exclude unqualified persons acting as advocates.
But that question arises only because of the postulated hole in s 106.
To invent a hole in an unqualified prohibition in a public statute, just to invoke a supposed ancient and inherent power in someone else partly to plug that hole, would be very roundabout.
That is like postulating that the Legislature had deliberately built a dyke against the sea with a hole in it, because they knew that a little boy might come along and stick his finger in the hole.
Consequences of Violating Legal Professions Act In Professional Sign Crafters (1988) Ltd. v.
Wedekind, 1994 CarswellAlta 90, 153 A.R.
L.R.
(3d) 387 (Q.B.), the statement of claim of the corporate plaintiff was prepared and issued by David Stanley, the sole director and officer of the plaintiffs.
When considering the consequences of corporations violating the Legal Professions Act regarding the commencement of an action, O'Leary J. said at pp.
63-64: Section 103(1) of the Act forbids the commencement of an action in the Court of Queen's Bench by an individual who is not a member of the Law Society.
Subsection (2) exempts certain individuals and circumstances from that prohibition.
A corporation cannot act “in person” within subs.
(2)(h) and no other exemption applies.
A corporation is a legal entity separate from its shareholders, directors, officers and employees and none of them can commence an action on behalf of the corporation without contravening s.

I agree with the Master's conclusion that Stanley violated the Act when he prepared, issued and served the Statement of Claim on behalf of the Plaintiffs … The purpose of the Act is to protect the public by preventing unqualified individuals from practicing law.
Those who contravene the Act are subject to penalties.
There is nothing express or implied in the statute imposing any sanctions on those for whom unqualified individuals purport to act.
In many cases the “clients” will be ignorant of the lack of qualifications and it would be harsh to strike out their actions as nullities.
I cannot imagine a valid reason for doing so … In my opinion, there is no justification in principle or practice for declaring the action a nullity.
The Court has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject-matter.
It is not suggested that the Statement of Claim is defective in form or that it does not disclose a cause of action.
The Defendants have suffered no prejudice which cannot be remedied in costs.
There is no policy reason for declaring the action a nullity.
The provisions of the Act can be enforced against those who contravene its terms without the necessity of striking out the underlying proceedings.

In my opinion the proper disposition of this application is to direct a stay of the action until such time as the Plaintiffs are represented on the record by a qualified agent as required by the Act and the Rules of Court.
The Rule Does Not Permit Violation of the Legal Profession Act In Chapman Estate v.
Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 58, 2015 CarswellAlta 187, 3 E.T.R.
(4th) 211, an individual was the co-executor of an estate which had as one of its assets a judgment obtained by Mr.
Chapman prior to his death.
The co-executor was not permitted to appear in Court to represent the estate in judgment enforcement proceedings.
Madam Justice Veldhuis said, at paragraphs 2–4: 2 Mr.
Oommen appeared before several justices of the Court of Queen's Bench without incident.
However, at one appearance before Michalyshyn J, Mr.
Oommen was told that the Legal Profession Act, RSA 2000, c L-8 prevented him from appearing in court on behalf of the estate.
The Court issued an order to that effect which also dismissed Mr.
Oommen's substantive application to review a garnishment order.
Mr.
Oommen appealed that order, and appeared before me in chambers seeking the right to appear on behalf of the estate in the Court of Appeal.
I dismissed his application: Oommen v Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 34.
Mr.
Oommen is now applying for permission to appeal my decision to a panel of this Court.
3 It is unfortunate that Mr.
Oommen was permitted to appear in the Court of Queen's Bench on several occasions prior to being told that he could not represent the Chapman estate.
The Legal Profession Act does not permit Mr.
Oommen, either as a co-executor, co-beneficiary, personal representative or litigation representative to appear in court on behalf of the estate of Mr.
Chapman.
This action can only proceed through the courts if the estate is represented by someone authorized to appear for others in accordance with the Legal Profession Act.
Mr.
Oommen is not one of these people.
There is also no authority in the Survival of Actions Act, RSA 2000, c S-27, for the proposition that Mr.
Oommen can act for the estate in court.
That Act only establishes that a cause of action survives for the benefit of an estate, and allows for the appointment of a litigation representative.
It says nothing of who can appear in court for an estate.
4 Rule 2.23 of the Rules of Court allows a court to grant permission to a person to assist a litigant, but this appointment cannot conflict with s 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act.
The law is clear that Mr.
Oommen cannot act for this estate in court.

There are many reasons why only those licenced to practice law may appear on behalf of others (amongst them the fact that lawyers are professionally trained, and insured against negligence for the benefit of clients).
These are sound policy reasons that support the legislative framework.
Discretion to grant right of audience to non-lawyer In Vuong Van Tai Holding v.

Alberta (Minister of Justice and Solicitor General), 2020 ABCA 169, 2020 CarswellAlta 793, Justice Slatter noted the effect of the 2020 amendment to the rule: [15] Rule 2.23(4) of the Rules of Court has now restored the discretion of the Court to allow a right of audience to a non-lawyer: see Pacer Enterprises Ltd v Cummings, 2004 ABCA 28 at para.
8, 26 Alta LR (4th) 241, 346 AR 161, citing Professional Sign Crafters (1988) Ltd. v Wedekind (1994), 1994 CanLII 9245 (AB QB), 19 Alta LR (3d) 53 at pp.

57-8, 153 AR 358: In order to place the issues in perspective it is important to distinguish between the inherent discretion of a superior Court to permit a non-lawyer to appear physically in Court or before a judge as a representative or advocate of another person (the “right of audience”), and the right of an individual to represent another person in respect of legal matters generally, that is, the right to practice law The Court now has a discretion to permit an individual to speak in court on behalf of a corporation.
Clause 5 of the order of October 8, 2015 is accordingly rescinded.
To be clear, the enactment of R.
2.23(4) does not mean that non-lawyers have an unlimited right to represent corporations.
The presumption is still that corporations must be represented by lawyers.
Rule 2.23(4) merely restores the discretion of judges to give a right of audience in court to non-lawyers connected to the corporation: Pacer Enterprises at para.

paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)

sentences.text: Lawyer of record

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.24 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) The lawyer or firm of lawyers whose name appears on a commencement document, pleading, affidavit or other document filed or served in an action as acting for a party is a lawyer of record for that party. (2) When there is a lawyer of record, the party for whom the lawyer of record acts may not self-represent unless the Court permits. (3) A lawyer of record remains a lawyer of record until the lawyer ceases to be a lawyer of record under these rules.

paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.26 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) If a person who is served with a commencement document, pleading or other document asks a lawyer or firm of lawyers if the lawyer or firm is a lawyer of record in an action, application or proceeding, the lawyer must respond to the question in writing as soon as practicable. (2) If a lawyer or firm of lawyers whose name appears as a lawyer of record in an action denies being the lawyer of record, (a) every application and proceeding in the action is stayed, and (b) no further application, proceeding or step may be taken in the action without the Court's permission.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.27:1 Rule 2.27 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.27. 1. The Rule Does Not Allow a Party to Bypass the Rules on Service In 1920341 Alberta Ltd. v. Jonsson, 2018 ABCA 231, 2018 CarswellAlta 1243, Justice Slatter said: 8 Counsel who filed the application for permission to appeal described themselves as “Counsel for the purpose of filing leave to appeal only”. Rule 2.27 recognizes the validity of retainers for specified purposes, but there are limits on the use of this procedure. In this case counsel who filed the Memorandum gave their own address as the address for service. Rule 11.15 allows any other party to serve a litigant at the address for service. Alberta law does not recognize the concept of “refusing service”: Zahmol Properties Ltd. v Calgary (City), 2012 ABCA 89 at para. 18, 522 AR 32, 62 Alta LR (5th) 253. Thus, the respondents were entitled to serve their memoranda of argument in opposition to the application on that firm, and were not obliged to try and serve 1920341 by any other method: Sandhu v MEG Place LP Investment Corp., 2012 ABCA 266 at paras. 21, 24-5, 542 AR 12. Rule 2.27 does not allow parties to bypass the rules on service.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.28 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) A party may change the party's lawyer of record or may self-represent by (a) serving a notice of the change in Form 3 on every other party and on the lawyer or former lawyer of record, and (b) filing an affidavit of service of the notice. (3) The notice must include an address for service. (4) The notice is not required to be served on (a) a party noted in default, or (b) a party against whom default judgment has been entered.

paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.29 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to rule 2.31, a lawyer or firm of lawyers may withdraw as lawyer of record by (a) serving on the client and each of the other parties a notice of withdrawal in Form 4 that states (i) the client's last known address, and (ii) that on the expiry of 10 days after the date on which the affidavit of service of the notice is filed, the withdrawing lawyer will no longer be the lawyer of record, and (b) filing an affidavit of service of the notice. (2) The withdrawal of the lawyer of record takes effect 10 days after the affidavit of service of the notice is filed. (3) The address of the party stated in the notice of withdrawal is the party's address for service after the lawyer of record withdraws unless another address for service is provided or the Court otherwise orders. (4) The Court may on application order that a lawyer need not disclose the last known address of a client and instead may provide an alternative address for service for the client in a notice of withdrawal served under this rule where the Court considers it necessary to protect the safety and well-being of the client. (5) An application under subrule (4) may be made without notice.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.29:1 Rule 2.29 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.29. How Not to Withdraw as Counsel In Baron Real Estate Investments Ltd. v. Edmonton (Subdivision and Development Appeal Board), 2018 ABCA 67, 2018 CarswellAlta 301, a lawyer purported to withdraw as counsel of record by delivering a letter to the Court of Appeal on the day of a scheduled hearing before the Court. Justice Wakeling pointed out the error in that procedure. 22 Counsel for Baron Real Estate did not appear on Wednesday. Instead, counsel informed the Court in a letter received by the Registry at 9:39 am that he withdrew as lawyer of record. 23 A lawyer does not withdraw as lawyer of record by delivering a letter to the court. Rule 2.29(1) of the Alberta Rules of Court23 provides an unambiguous protocol. The lawyer who wishes to withdraw must file a notice of withdrawal and serve it on the parties and file an affidavit of service. Rule 2.29(2) provides that “[t]he withdrawal of the lawyer of record takes effect 10 days after the affidavit of service of the notice is filed”. 24 As a result, Baron Real Estate's lawyer of record was not in attendance when his client's application was called. Given that Baron Real Estate is a corporation, neither its officers nor shareholders were entitled to speak on its behalf ….

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.31 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: Commentary § 2.31:1 Rule 2.31 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.31. In Fitzpatrick v. College of Physical Therapists of Alberta, 2020 ABCA 88, 2020 CarswellAlta 386, after the appeal date was set, the appellants' counsel sought leave to withdraw for non-payment of their account. Justice Hughes granted the application after setting out and balancing the factors to consider: [4] In R v Cunningham, 2010 SCC 10, a case which concerned the withdrawal of counsel, the Supreme Court held that courts have inherent jurisdiction to control their own process, along with the authority to exercise control over counsel when necessary to protect that process. Other principles from Cunningham include the following: 1) Leave to withdraw should be granted where the application is made well in advance of any scheduled proceeding and adjournment is unnecessary: Cunningham at para 47. 2) If timing is an issue the court may grant permission to withdraw if counsel seeks to withdraw for ethical reasons. Ethical reasons do not include the non-payment of fees: Cunningham at para 48. 3) When counsel seek to withdraw because of the non-payment of fees, the court may exercise its discretion to refuse leave to withdraw but should only do so after considering the following non-exhaustive list of factors (Cunningham at para 50): • whether it is feasible for the individual to represent him or herself; • other means of obtaining counsel; • whether counsel gave reasonable notice to the party to allow the individual to seek other means of representation; • impact on the respondent; and • the history of the proceedings including whether the party has changed counsel repeatedly. [5] The Supreme Court also observed that rules enacted by law societies are “essential statements of the appropriate standards of professional conduct”: Cunningham at para 36. [6] The relevant sections of the Law Society of Alberta's Code of Conduct are: 3.7-1 A lawyer must not withdraw from representation of a client except for good cause and on reasonable notice to the client. … 3.7-3 If, after reasonable notice, the client fails to provide a retainer or funds on account of disbursements or fees, a lawyer may withdraw unless serious prejudice to the client would result. … [11] The last factor to consider is harm to the administration of justice should the appeal not proceed on April 9, 2020. This factor weighs against the granting of the application in that the time this appeal is currently scheduled for, may not be able to be used by another appeal. …

Other principles from Cunningham include the following: 1) Leave to withdraw should be granted where the application is made well in advance of any scheduled proceeding and adjournment is unnecessary: Cunningham at para 47.
2) If timing is an issue the court may grant permission to withdraw if counsel seeks to withdraw for ethical reasons.
Ethical reasons do not include the non-payment of fees: Cunningham at para 48.

3) When counsel seek to withdraw because of the non-payment of fees, the court may exercise its discretion to refuse leave to withdraw but should only do so after considering the following non-exhaustive list of factors (Cunningham at para 50): • whether it is feasible for the individual to represent him or herself; • other means of obtaining counsel; • whether counsel gave reasonable notice to the party to allow the individual to seek other means of representation; • impact on the respondent; and • the history of the proceedings including whether the party has changed counsel repeatedly.
[5] The Supreme Court also observed that rules enacted by law societies are “essential statements of the appropriate standards of professional conduct”: Cunningham at para 36.

[6] The relevant sections of the Law Society of Alberta's Code of Conduct are: 3.7-1 A lawyer must not withdraw from representation of a client except for good cause and on reasonable notice to the client. … 3.7-3 If, after reasonable notice, the client fails to provide a retainer or funds on account of disbursements or fees, a lawyer may withdraw unless serious prejudice to the client would result. … [11] The last factor to consider is harm to the administration of justice should the appeal not proceed on April 9, 2020.

paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 2.32 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 2 (Part 2)
paragraphs.text: (1) A lawyer or firm of lawyers ceases to be the lawyer of record if (a) in the case of an individual lawyer, (i) the lawyer dies, (ii) the lawyer is suspended or disbarred from practice as a lawyer, or (iii) the lawyer ceases to practise as a lawyer; (b) in the case of a firm of lawyers, the firm dissolves. (2) If any of the circumstances described in subrule (1) occurs, any party may apply to the Court, without notice to any other party, for directions respecting service of documents. (3) The Court may (a) direct the manner in which service is to be effected, (b) dispense with service in accordance with rule 11.29, or (c) make any other order respecting service that the circumstances require. (4) An order under this rule applies until a notice is given under rule 2.28 or 2.29 or the Court otherwise orders. (5) Nothing in this rule prevents a party from serving a notice of change of lawyer of record or notice that the party intends to self-represent.
